utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel Williams, would you please state your complete name, your rank, your career path, and your education. "Career path" meaning your Bosniak experience and any foreign experience to being in Britain.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: My full name is Peter Gage Williams. I am a full Colonel in the British army. My educational experience, I have a degree in history from the University of Cambridge, and I have attended several military staff colleges, most recently the Australian Defense College in 1999, and I have served three times in the former Yugoslavia, on the first occasion between May -- well, November 1993 and May 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you have any specialised military training?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In addition to being an infantry officer, I have considerable experience including training courses in the fields of intelligence and in liaison duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with any foreign languages?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: At one stage of my career I qualified as a Russian interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you describe your period of time in Bosnia, from when to when, and the nature of the operation?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was the Commander Officer of a British Army infantry battalion, the 1st Battalion, the Coldstream Guards, which undertook an operation known in the British military as Operation Grapple 3. This was from the period the 8th of November, 1993 to the 8th of May, 1994. My battalion took over from the 1st Battalion, the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment of Yorkshire.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was the mission of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The mission of the battalion was to provide support for the delivery of humanitarian assistance both into and through Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any formula for the division of such support?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was no overall formula for this. The rules and allocation of humanitarian aid was decided by the UNHCR, which was the lead agency. For example, in the area of Greater Vitez, the division was 70 percent to the Croat population and 30 percent to the Muslim minority. This was based on figures, an assessment by UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you aware of how the supplies came to the -- how the humanitarian aid supplies came to the population that was to be served? What was the route?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: At the period of in time, there was only one road, route into Central Bosnia. This came from Split, through the Croatian border to the town of Tomislav Grand and then moved from there up through the Vrbas valley, Gornji Vakuf, and then on to the Lasva Valley in the area of Vitez, and moved on to the UNHCR depot in Zenica, from which it was then secondarily distributed with security provide by UNPROFOR troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there any other means of receiving this food for the Muslim community?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was no other way that any substantive quantities of aid could reach Central Bosnia other than along this one route.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was your battalion aware of any reports as to other means for the Croat community to receive assistance?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Although we had no physical proof of this, it was undoubtedly a fact that there was black marketeering that was bringing goods, particularly fuel and cigarettes, into the area of Kiseljak. This was coming up through the Republika Srpska, the Serb-held areas of Bosnia, and then on occasion some of this fuel and other supplies appeared to be making its way into the Vitez Croat area, although I would hasten to say that none of this seemed to be benefiting the general population, Croat population of the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who was it benefiting, do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I can only assume it was benefiting the leadership. For example, on one occasion, we were forced to investigate the theft of nearly 36 tonnes or some 36 tonnes of fuel that had been brought under U.N. auspices from Kiseljak to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any price ranges for fuel in the Kiseljak area? Did any figures come to your attention?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was reputed, although, obviously, we didn't need to buy fuel and so had no proof of this ourselves, it was reputed that the fuel in Kiseljak area was not dissimilarly priced from fuel in Herzegovina and Croatia proper.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask the witness to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask the Registrar to distribute to the witness and to all others in the courtroom appropriate the packet of exhibits to which I will make reference by exhibit number and date. Colonel Williams, before you is a packet of documents, which you have seen before, and have indicated that these documents relate to your period of time, and in fact your mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And relative to questions, I will ask you, please, to look for documents, and I will just ask you to highlight a few points in them. If you would please look for what is 17 November, 1993, marked Z1308.1, and also pull Z1322.1, which is 2 December, and Z1323.1, which is 6 December. Some of the figures with whom you had to deal, with whom your battalion, if not you yourself, had to deal, are referred to in the various documents, which I have asked you to take a look at. In the document Z1308.1, under the Vitez entry, there are comments about Mario Cerkez. Are you familiar with the role that Mario Cerkez was to have played?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I am familiar with his role, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you also familiar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In that same milinfosum, there is a reference in paragraph 3 under the Vitez section to a Chris Wilson. Are you familiar with Chris Wilson?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, I had no dealings with this person.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document was from 2 December, 1322.1. Again, another personality in the area was Ivica Rajic. And the comment on the third page would be under Busovaca, point 14. Did you have any personal dealings with Ivica Rajic, or was this information simply brought to your attention because you were the Commanding Officer?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I had no dealings with Ivica Rajic. This was simply brought to my attention as Commanding Officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That he was back in his --

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Allegedly, he was back in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In his area. Thank you very much. And then the December 6th document, 1323.1, paragraph 5 under the Vitez entry. There is a passage which indicates that there was difficulty in getting past certain points along Route Diamond, and the authority of Mario Cerkez was invoked by locals. Was it common, in your understanding, to have general orders less regarded than orders by local officials?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If I may, I would point out that the crossing to Kruscica was not on Route Diamond --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: -- per se. Nevertheless, there were difficulties on occasion at checkpoints because, either the message that had been passed down from the chain of command, either the message had not arrived at the checkpoint, or, possibly, there was activity at the checkpoint that was of a more locally controlled nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Therefore, the entry that the HVO troops stated that they would only take orders from Mario Cerkez, Commander of Viteska HVO Brigade, was not uncommon?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was a particular problem in the Kruscica area. In most other areas, I would submit that the -- particularly on the HVO side, the chain of command was normally successful in the transmission of its orders to individual checkpoints. This particular front line was throughout the period of fighting a particularly difficult one, to achieve crossings by United Nations, liaison officers, and indeed this continued for some time after the ceasefire between the HVO and the Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You had occasion to meet Colonel Blaskic during your tenure there. Could you describe the types of meetings and the frequency of your meetings?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I met Colonel Blaskic probably on half a dozen or more occasions. He was clearly the Military Commander of a tactical type within the Central Bosnian area, in particular the Vitez pocket where we were based. And I met him more often than not in the Hotel Vitez, which played a war headquarters role, as far as we could ascertain, within the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to meet with Colonel Kordic -- with Mr. Kordic and Colonel Blaskic at the same time?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: On a number of occasions, I would suspect three or possibly four occasions, I met Mr. Kordic when Colonel Blaskic was also present.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What were your observations, if you have any, about the nature of the relationship, in terms of authority, whom over whom?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It had been brought to my attention by Colonel Duncan, my predecessor, and it was very much my impression as well, that in the presence of Mr. Kordic, Colonel Blaskic played a deferential role and always looked up to Mr. Kordic as if he was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was your impression of Colonel Blaskic's leadership style?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic, a relatively young man to be in command of such a large area, and I would describe his leadership style as being of a very formal nature. He was not leading -- in my view -- by example, but more by sheer authority of his position. He did not feel the need, I felt, to -- in comparison to his Deputy, Colonel Filipovic, to try to lead by personal example.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Turning your attention to 16 November 1993, and asking you to look at documents which would be from 16 November 93, Z1305.2, and 1305 -- I think we'll start with 1305.2. Can you describe, please, the meeting, which is the subject of the particular milinfosum?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This is the meeting with Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was discussed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the reference, please, on the document to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: One moment, please. It would be on page 2, the Busovaca area as discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Page 2 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Additionally, to facilitate perhaps a transition, if I could ask everyone to take out from November 16th, Z1305.4, which will have use elsewhere as well. I would like to ask your impression of anything peculiar or that struck you as unusual about the seating arrangement at these meetings, and particularly this meeting.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: On this occasion, Mr. Kordic was accompanied by Mr. Kostroman. Mr. Kordic was very much in control, and as on other occasions, when Colonel Blaskic was present as well, Mr. Kordic always sat in the centre and was with the other members on his flanks, demonstrating, I believe, the fact that he was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you recall how Colonel Kordic was dressed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: On this occasion, Mr. Kordic was wearing military-style camouflage clothing, in particular a camouflage waistcoat. On this occasion, indeed any occasion I recall, he was definitely wearing an HVO arm patch on his arm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In general, when you saw him, how was he dressed? In general.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In general, during the period of the armed conflict here in Central Bosnia, I never saw him other than dressed in what I would describe as a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: One of the topics for discussion at this meeting concerned the Vitezit factory. Can you give some background to the problems that were posed specifically to the British Battalion with this factory?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The Vitezit factory is a large complex just to the south of the Vitez town itself and was the major explosives factory located within Bosnia-Herzegovina. It contained many thousands of tonnes, so it was told us to, many thousands of tonnes of manufactured explosive, and was within the tower, the steam towers or chimney. It was in easy sight of all three of the U.N. bases that were in the general area of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you able to give an idea, roughly, in kilometres the distances of various bases and UNPROFOR interests from the factory?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The nearest base was the battalion logistic centre, which was within about one and a half to two kilometres from the factory, but the main headquarters of the battalion was in Stara Bila, which is about four kilometres, I would think, from the factory complex. And the Dutch-Netherlands transport company was in Santici, which is a little further, perhaps as much as five kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who was controlling this particular factory?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The factory was controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what were the particular concerns about the factory that had been brought to your attention?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was brought to my attention, as we arrived in Central Bosnia, in the middle of November, that there was a threat that the factory would be destroyed in the event of the Bosnian Army capturing the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There are a number of documents which are relevant to this particular issue, and one of them I have already asked you to take out, it is 1305.4. I can ask at this point the relevant documents to the next few questions are Z1299.1, which is 12 November, 1993; Z1315.2, which is 22 November. Then there is summary of Z1315.3. It's a bit large, and it may be toward the back. It's unclear how it's dated. If it is not in the packet, my apologies. We'll have to supply it later. I'm sorry. It is in the packet Ms. Verhaag informs me. Then Z1290 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You'll have to wait a moment while we find these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You referred to 1315.3.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. That is of -- it is a summary of incidents. It is undated. It just says "November 1993," and in the upper corner, by hand, it is written "7 June, 1998." But it is the 1993 information which is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't have this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I apologise. It is probably behind the 13 November -- I'm sorry, behind 1315.2. Right behind 1315.2. There is, additionally, behind these, 1290.1, which is a letter on letterhead from the Slobodan Princip Seljo factory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That should be dated the 9th of November. Then 1315.4, which is an assessment of threat. It is a packet of 22 November. Then 1318.1 from the 28th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Nice, I've been -- throughout this case I've been concerned with the way that these documents are being produced. Now, I understand, of course, that you have a mass of documents which you're going to look through and having them produced, but the way that these documents are handled in this Tribunal is far from satisfactory. The Court should not have to scrabble through the documents trying to find them. They should be produced in a bundle and handed in. You are familiar with such a scheme, and I don't understand why in this Tribunal it can't be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Generally it is done and generally they come to you, think I, in an orderly way. I suspect that on this particular occasion some other documents had to be added at a late minute and that's why they're not strictly in the order of presentation. Most of them are but there are one or two out of order. I happen to know that the staff concerned have been working over the weekend. And, of course, documents can't be produced until the witnesses are spoken to and have the matters discussed with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have no doubt that people have been working very hard. It is the method of presentation which concerns me. Perhaps you could take this back to the Office of the Prosecutor. The documents should be produced, particularly a bundle like this, in a folder or a lever-arch file, so that the Court and everybody else, the witness and the Defence, can find their way through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Insofar as their shortcomings today, we will do our best to ensure they don't occur again, and I'm sorry you have been inconvenienced today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not just today. I've noticed this and in other cases. It seems to be the practice that documents are produced out of order and then the Court has to try and find its way around. Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I please apologise personally. Mr. Nice was really not a part of this particular plan. May I explain to you that the reason simply is that documents cover more than one issue, so we felt that the only way that we could present them so they wouldn't get lost is chronologically. Excuse us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is no need to apologise personally, Ms. Somers. It's a general comment and that's why it was directed at Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you, Your Honour. Again, continuing in a bit of a wade-through but important, is -- I think I left off at the 28th of November, which was a threat assessment document, Z1318.1. And Z1305.4, which goes back -- I believe it was possibly discussed earlier. It is the 16th of November -- yes. I had mentioned it. You already have it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Ms. Somers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Then Z1320.2, which is 30 November. And that should be sufficient for this line of questions. Additionally, there is a video which we have presented to the audio section, and I would like to show it before we get into any further discussion, but I am obligated to inform the Chamber that it was produced by ITN out of London with a number of extreme conditions for the -- generally for the Tribunal, limiting copying, distribution. I had assured them that I would make it known. So if I can submit it to the registry for the record, I'd appreciate that. If we can ask that the video be presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I inquire if there is a transcript available for everybody's review?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No there's not. This was just Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, could I ask you why there was no translation? Maybe this question should be addressed to the Registrar. There is no transcript, there is no translation. So I don't consider this presentation to be normal, the way in which this video has been presented. I am able to follow in English, of course, but still, sometimes I do need a translation, for the sake of precision. And I find that this way of presenting the video is not normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I address that. Our apologies. However, we received this particular video Friday from ITN. It was a bit difficult to obtain it, for some logistical reasons, and we simply were unavailable to submit it timely. If the Court would grant us leave to provide a transcript for subsequent use, we would be happy to do so. And we had no opportunity even to have it translated into Croatian as well. Our apologies. Again, it was a timing issue. The first time I saw it was 2 on Friday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While we are dealing with that, what was the date? I may have missed it. What was the date of the broadcast?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel Williams, my understanding is this is 22nd of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is that acceptable to Your Honour Judge Bennouna, to provide a -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am waiting for the transcript, which must be a complete transcript of what was said in the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we a number for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Z1315.5.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you comment on what was just shown, and what measures were taken by the British Battalion to assess the real threat, if it were in fact real, and to deal with it in an authoritative manner?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The film, as seen, you will notice that under normal British rules I was not encouraged to be doomsday-ish about this threat in public, because this would obviously lead to confusion and unnecessary fear amongst the families of soldiers back in Germany. Nevertheless, an opportunity arose to visit the factory, in fact on the day that this very broadcast was made back in Britain on the 22nd of November, and I visited the factory with a qualified explosives ordnance disposal officer, Captain Bassett. The reason we visited is outlined in the letter from the factory. The factory claimed that there was a risk, unless fuel was provided by the United Nations, that the explosives processes would become unsafe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is that the letter which is marked Z1290.1 from the 9th of November, 1993, the top of which is on the letterhead from the factory?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It is indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was the response to the request for fuel and to the request for evacuation?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In order to respond to this request, we asked to be given the opportunity to inspect the factory and its explosive manufacturing processes, so that our own experts from the Royal Engineers could make an assessment as to the necessity of providing such fuel. This inspection visit occurred on the 22nd of November, in the company of the director of the factory, but there were no HVO personnel present during this inspection. We found the factory to indeed be prepared for destruction, but the technical assessment was that the processes themselves would remain safe, and that it was, we believed, an attempt to get United Nations to provide fuel that would then be misdirected to other purposes. For this reason, the request for fuel from the United Nations was subsequently turned down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which document contains the assessment of the British Battalion authorities as to the reality of the threat?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There's an initial technical assessment, which is Z1315.4.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And then is there a subsequent?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Subsequent to that there is Z1318.1, which was the final technical assessment, what we send on to our own headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It appears from the milinfosums that are before you, that the threat was repeated on the 12th of November, 1993. And in Z1299.1 there is a reference, under "Vitez," paragraph number 5, to a comment by Cerkez. In connection with the Vitezit ammunition factory, Cerkez claimed that if the factory would be blown up, it would have little effect on BritBat. Did that appear to be true?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The question as to whether there would be little effect was really based, principally, on whether or not the warning that had been promised by the HVO would be forthcoming. But in truth, had there been little or no warning, there would, as per the technical assessments, have been a considerable risk, not only to the U.N. military, but more particularly, perhaps, to the civil population in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We have seen that there was comment on the matter by Blaskic, Cerkez. And turning to Z1305.4, which is an LO report of the meeting of the 16th November. What was the general comment by Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic confirmed what had already been mentioned by Colonel Blaskic and others, that indeed there was -- there would be a requirement to destroy the factory, albeit attempts would be made to minimise the risk to the United Nations forces, but that it could not be lost.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. And did Mr. Kordic comment about whether or not there would be any efforts to proceed with this or to avoid it?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't think he commented on this occasion, as to whether it was more or less likely, but the fundamental issue here was that the Bosnian Army had several munitions factories in the area, and Bugogno and in Novi Travnik, and the one missing link in their own munition system was the provision of explosives. And that, of course, would have been -- that missing link would have been filled, had the Bosnian army seized the ammunition factory, the explosives factory in Vitezit. And it is that reason, as per the words of Colonel Blaskic on the television clip there, that if the factory was lost to the Bosnian Army, they would then be well placed to carry on the war with vigour against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On the milinfosum dated 30 November, which is Z1320.2. On the second page under "Busovaca," page 2, paragraph 9, there is a comment about the BiH using chemical shells. Was there any investigation by BritBat, and if so, what were the results or conclusions?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Claims of this sort were made on several occasions, and on every occasion that they were made, we, in BritBat, volunteered to conduct a technical assessment of the alleged incidents. And on those occasions that these investigations were both permitted and carried out, our own explosives experts claimed that there was no evidence of chemically-filled shells being used.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there a request about evacuation of the civilian population, and if so, from whom and what area, what radius was covered by that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We were not aware of any request to evacuate civilian population with respect to the Vitezit factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you communicate with any superior officers about the threat, and if so, what was the nature of the communication, and what were the results?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We were so concerned by the repeated voicings of this threat to explode the factory, that we passed our concern in a letter to the chief of staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina command, pointing out that although we were not lawyers, we were convinced that to do -- if the factory were indeed blown up, it would surely constitute some sort of a war crime, and indeed even the threat of doing so might, perhaps, be seen as in some way in contravention of some legal provision. It was our concern -- we asked the chief of staff to write to Mr. Kordic in order to voice the concerns of the U.N.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did Brigadier Ramsay involve himself at any point in the issue of the explosives factory?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I can ask those who have the documents, please to pull a document from 2 January, Z1347.1, labelled "warning," with the seal -- an HVO seal on it. Then from 4 January, Z1349.2. It appears to be to Brigadier Ramsay. Then there is another document, a letter, from Brigadier Ramsay of 4 January. The top probably has the Croatian date. It is addressed to Colonel Blaskic. It is 1349.3. If these documents are familiar to you, could you please discuss them?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: These documents are familiar. Indeed, they lead me to point out that I was incorrect a moment ago in suggesting that Brigadier Ramsay had written to Mr. Kordic. Quite clearly, from the documents, the correspondence went to Colonel Blaskic. But, indeed, the correspondence did take place between Brigadier Ramsay and Colonel Blaskic, warning him that the destruction of this factory would indeed constitute a war crime, in the opinion of headquarters Bosnia-Herzegovina command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just turning your attention to the warning letter from Colonel Blaskic, from the 2nd, which is 1347.1. There is a reference in paragraph 6 to an evacuation. Do you recall this particular request?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was never a request to the British Battalion to undertake any evacuation of the population. Indeed, this point is made, I believe, in the letter from -- in the second paragraph in the letter from Brigadier Ramsay, that such an evacuation lay outside the mandate of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And that would be the document of 1349.3, the letter from Brigadier Ramsay of the 4th of January. Thank you. Did you ever hear the threat repeated by Colonel Blaskic to you after these incidents?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: After this time, no, Colonel Blaskic never raised this issue again with the UNPROFOR forces in the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether or not Colonel Blaskic was present in Central Bosnia when this correspondence was undertaken?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There is reason -- we have reason to believe that Colonel Blaskic left the Vitez area by helicopter at night, probably on the night of the 2nd, 3rd of January, and that he was later reported by the Croatian press, meeting the HVO commander in chief, General Roso, and we believed that he returned again by night, probably on or about the 13th of January.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And is this the information that's referred to in milinfosum Z1348 from the 3rd of January -- I'm sorry, 1348.1, 3 January, paragraph 3, under the heading "Vitez"?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This is correct. This is the first report that Colonel Blaskic had more than likely left the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. There was a meeting at which Dario Kordic, Ignac Kostroman, Ivan Santic, Tihomir Blaskic, and yourself were present on the 3rd of February. Looking at the milinfosum -- I believe it is a milinfosum -- from the 3rd of February, which is Z1365.1. There is a comment by Kostroman that I would ask you to comment on, if you recall it.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: To put the meeting in perspective, General Cot, who was the commander of UNPROFOR within the whole of Yugoslavia, at that time visited Vitez. I took him on the 2nd of February to meet Colonel Cuskic in Travnik, who was the local Bosnian army commander, and for reasons of balance, and I believed good manners, invited Mr. Kordic and his cohorts to meet with General Cot the following day. A meeting was held, and once again Mr. Kordic clearly played the part of the leader in this group, sitting in the centre, speaking first. And then Mr. Kostroman made some remarks concerning the Vitezit factory. He repeated the threat to destroy the ammunition factory despite the consequences, and then made remarks about 7.000 Mujahedin being present in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm asking you to look at a letter, Z1363, which is dated 25 January. The translation should appear on top. It is from an Anto Puljic. Two points about this letter, one of which is that it again concerns mention of the Vitezit or the Princip factory. The second is the persons to whose attention the letter on this subject matter was sent. Would you read them, kindly, into the record?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The letter has been sent by Mr. Puljic, first to Mr. Sliskovic, who is described as the assistant commander for security.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. A. Sliskovic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. A. Sliskovic, the Assistant Ccommander for security in the Vitez military district. And the other addressee is Mr. Colonel Dario Kordic, who is described in the letter as the Assistant Chief of the main staff of the Armed Forces of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At that -- it says Mr. Colonel Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Originally it would appear to say Gospodin Pukovni.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At that time, who was the Chief of the HVO staff?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: At that time, I assume that this was General Roso.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On the issue of casualty evacuation as well as generally on the issue of agreements for delivery of humanitarian aid, can you recall, about the 2nd of February, was there to be an evacuation of non-combatants and did it take place?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There had been considerable attempts to ensure that injured persons, non-military persons or persons of non-military age, could be removed from the area of Stari Vitez, which was a besieged enclave, Muslim enclave, within the Vitez -- the Croat-dominated Vitez pocket. We had tried on a number of occasions to remove injured civilians from Stari Vitez. More often than not we were unsuccessful. On this occasion, after some considerable dealings, we had an arrangement that on the 2nd of February, we could move both injured persons from Stari Vitez to Zenica, and from the Croat hospital at Nova Bila to the Croat medical facilities in Kiseljak. This was also linked in with the delivery of aid on the 70/30 proportion as arranged by the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did the parties, especially the Croats, honour this agreement?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The agreement, having been laboured over for many days, on the 2nd of February there was a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could you discuss the problem?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The -- I was informed that there was a problem and moved as fast as I could to the HVO headquarters in the Hotel Vitez. As I arrived, it was brought to my attention that Colonel Blaskic drove off from the back door in his jeep. I was then confronted by his deputy, Colonel Filipovic, and Colonel Filipovic told me that there could be no casualty evacuation on that date, that there could only be the movement of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was your response to that partial fulfilment?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was horrified and told Colonel Filipovic that I knew he had been left to pass on an unacceptable message by Colonel Blaskic, whom I had seen leaving at the back door; that I could tell from the excuse that he suggested that he didn't believe the excuse either, and I gave him until midday to resolve the problem and turn back on both the movement of the casualties and of the humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you willing to only deliver the aid or to do partial?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I suggested that the excuse given by Colonel Filipovic was that it would be too dangerous for the HVO forces to allow both aid and civilian casualties to cross the front line out of Stari Vitez, the casualties out, the aid in. This would be too large a window and would be too dangerous for the HVO. I suggested that the casualties were, therefore, more important than the humanitarian aid, and that perhaps we should only do the casualties that day and not do the humanitarian aid. He told me that was an unacceptable alternative.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would only the Muslim community have been affected by the failure to deliver the humanitarian aid, or would there also have been an impact on the Croat community?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As on other occasions, I made it quite clear that we not deliver aid simply to one community. We were working under the instructions of UNHCR, and either we would feed the entire municipality with both its communities, Croat and Muslim, or we would feed no one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was the resolution, if any, by Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was rung sometime before midday, and a message was passed that Colonel Blaskic said that there must have been a misunderstanding and that the movement of both civilian casualties and humanitarian aid could go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did there appear to you, from your experience, that there was less incentive on the part of the Croats with regard to casualty evacuation?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The -- I think both sides were very keen to evacuate their casualties, which is quite understandable. The difference is that unlike humanitarian aid, where both parties were equally handicapped and both equally eager to receive humanitarian aid, in the case of casualties, the Croats enjoyed a particular advantage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which was?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The advantage was that unlike Stari Vitez, in which there were 1.200 people and no medical doctors -- indeed I believe the only medical support available was from a trained dental technician -- within the larger Croat pocket there was an adequate hospital in Nova Bila. For this reason, they had both good first-line medical support in November Bila, and they also enjoyed an advantage on the further evacuation of their casualties.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what would that advantage have been?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The advantage was that there were flights by Croatian army helicopters on a number of nights during this period into the Vitez pocket, and these flights allegedly brought in resupplies of one sort or another from Herzegovina and took out the casualties. We could only hear the helicopters coming and going, but it was clear from visits to Nova Bila hospital by my liaison officers that on the days following helicopter flights there were very few people left in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were these permissible, lawful helicopter flights?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No. All these helicopter flights were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please pause between answer and question for the translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If I could repeat myself. The flights were illegal under the terms of the U.N. Security Council resolution that had established a no-fly zone. And even on those occasions when the Croat authorities had sought permission under the no-fly regime, they had been turned down, but, nevertheless, the flights went ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel, you indicated, I believe, that these were Croatian helicopters. Are you suggesting they were HV helicopters?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Clearly in the dark, it's very difficult to tell where a helicopter came from. Nevertheless, we believed that the HVO in itself had no helicopters, that those helicopters that it was having the opportunity to use were Croatian army helicopters, and indeed on, I think, the 11th of March, we captured such a helicopter when it landed illegally in Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you attempted to negotiate or deal with the authorities, principally the HVO authorities, did you find that there was an unconditional approach to dealing?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there something called the concept of linkage attached to the dealings with the Croat authorities?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This was not, of course, unique, I would hasten to add, to the Croat authorities. It was also a feature of dealings with the Muslim authorities, but it was a particular problem where the Croat authorities were concerned, in that reciprocal humanitarian aid deliveries, for example, within the area of Novi Travnik, would be linked to other things such as the supply of water to Novi Travnik, which was beyond the gift of the United Nations to provide water through pipes to townships.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpreter. Was this an ongoing scenario?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was a continual and continuing problem throughout the period before the ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There is a document, Z1364.4. It has only "January 1994" on it. It is signed by a Major Tucker, and it describes linkages in BritBat AOR. If you could look at that, please. What is the significance of this document?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Document was produced by Major Tucker, who was my Operations Officer, and it was designed for passage up the chain of command to explain to people why nothing was ever as simple as perhaps it ought to be, and that things quite often from beyond our own area were impacting upon permission to carry out perfectly legitimate and indeed much needed humanitarian aid programmes. For example, there were two -- there was a helicopter held in Medjugorje, which is mentioned on the second page of this document whereby the BiH Army was refusing all manner of things, including prisoner of war exchanges, until its helicopter was released. But more immediately to us, there were issues within the Vitez pocket, the area controlled by the Croats, which were linked together. And as I've mentioned already, the provision of water to Novi Travnik, the Croat part of Novi Travnik, the non-delivery of water, the interruption of supply was used as an excuse for refusal to allow delivery of aid on occasion to Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what was the response, your response, to such suggestions?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We clearly wished to delink things wherever possible, and point out, as I said, that we were doing everything we could to find what was the problem was with the provision of water to Novi Travnik. It turned out that there was a cast iron type of some antiquity that had burst. The allegation by the Croat side that this must be sabotage by the Muslims, did not appear to be worthy of consideration. It was quite clearly metal fatigue. And we then struggled for some weeks to get a pipe of this diameter and type that we could place in and restore the water. But in our opinion, the interruption, the refusal to allow humanitarian aid into both communities in Novi Travnik, because of the interruption of the water supply, this was an unacceptable linkage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On the 21st of February -- sorry, let the interpreter catch up -- a meeting took place between International Community representatives and representatives of the HVO or the Bosnian Croat government. If you could turn your attention to Z1383.1, which is a milinfosum of 21 February, and Z1383.2, which appears to be a petition from 21 February, signed by various members of the International Community. If you could discuss the circumstances surrounding the meeting and the petition.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The petition, or demarche, perhaps more technically, was one that was delivered both to the Croat authorities. You have a copy of the original document here. It's a draft, but it is what was handed over. A similar document was also handed to Commander Alagic, the Commander of the Bosnian Army, 3rd Corps. At this stage, in the middle of February, there were overwhelming problems along this one and only route from Herzegovina, along which all the humanitarian aid convoys were moving. Within the Bosnian Army areas, there were problems with civilians attacking convoys, hungry civilians attacking convoys, hijacking loads, and there were other problems that were being caused by the Croat authorities. These included problems with snipers, particularly in the area of Gornji Vakuf. And there were problems with random harassing, artillery and mortar fire from HVO held territory onto villages along this route. And in the area of the Vitez pocket, there were problems where the Bosnian Croat police authorities were insisting on searching U.N. aid vehicles, despite this being in contravention of the agreements that the Croat authorities had signed up to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This document is signed by yourself Larry Hollingworth, who was -- if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This document was effectively an U.N. protest to the Croat authorities, signed by myself as the local military, U.N. military commander, by Mr. Hollingworth, who was the head of the UNHCR regional office in Zenica, and by Mr. J.F. Carter, who was the U.N. Civil Affairs Officer, who worked in the area as my battalion in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did Sir Martin Garrod play any role at this particular meeting, or was he essentially just witnessing?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sir Martin was effectively witnessing and observing, but he was fully in accord with all the points being made, and was very much a volunteer to come to the meeting to see the protest passed to the Croat authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was the reaction by the Croat side and undertakings, if any?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As it happened, the 21st of February was very close to the ceasefire agreement, which occurred some two days later. And we had probably left our protest a little too late, with the benefit of hindsight. Mr. Kordic listened to the protest and was -- I would describe him as unmoved by it all, and just dismissed most of it as being unimportant. Although his police chief, Mr. Rajic, was very upset at the criticism of the Croat police force, which I would point out was generally a well-organised and well-disciplined organisation, but on this occasion, I believe was exceeding its authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Had you ever discussed evacuations with Mr. Kordic himself, medical evacuations?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We discussed medical evacuations on this occasion on the 21st of February, but this was the second significant occasion on which I had discussed such evacuations with Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was the first one?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The first occasion was, I believe, on or around the 1st of December, but certainly much earlier during the period of armed conflict, when I had asked him to agree to the movement of two wounded children from Stari Vitez to the hospital in Zenica. And he had rejected this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was the ground for rejection?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic suggested that the children could go to the Croat medical facility in Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And why could they not go to a facility in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, I suggested that no Muslim mother would let her child out of Stari Vitez to go to a Croat facility, and the Croat facility was not a first-rate medical facility, whereas the hospital in Zenica was both in an area controlled by the Bosnian government and was a better hospital. And so I suggested that it would be much more sensible, for the well-being of these children, that they should move directly to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And was there a stated reason why they should not be moved to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic dismissed this by making what I took to be a very strange political statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which was?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He said that it would be -- in any case, it would be completely impossible for the children to go to Zenica, because such a move would constitute crossing an international border.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: From where to where?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He said this would be an international crossing, from the Croat republic of Herceg-Bosna to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you aware if these children ever were evacuated?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I can't say for certain whether these children ever were evacuated. It was certainly not -- if they were evacuated, it was in no way as a result of this meeting. My reaction to Mr. Kordic's statement about the crossing of an international border, I still recall my blood running cold and a ghastly feeling that no argument was clearly going to be sufficient to get these children to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The other occasion involving the evacuation of children, I believe was about the 21st of February, when this issue arose. Was there any comment made to you by Mr. Kordic about the evacuation of two Muslim children?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Following the reading of the protest letter that you have here, Mr. Kordic declared that now that the business is done, let's have lunch. And I said that we would like to see two children evacuated immediately from Stari Vitez. He said that was impossible. And I have to say I became rather angry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Returning to the issue of HV, or presumably HV helicopter flights. Are you able to give any type of history of the flights and what their purposes were, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The first flights that we had seen during our time were in mid-November, and occurred in broad daylight. One of them involved the dropping of bundles of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Into which territory?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Obviously, the intention was to drop the ammunition by parachute into the Croat held area, but some of the bundles actually fell into the Bosnian Army controlled area as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Somers. Sorry, I can't see you. Could you just return to the statement made by Mr. Kordic, that it was impossible to evacuate the two children. I'd like to find out from the Colonel whether he gave any explanation, any reason for the -- for this being impossible.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Your Honour, on that occasion, this was the 21st of February, the second occasion, no excuse was given. And I realised that my plea was going to be unsuccessful. But Sir Martin Garrod tried one last time, appealing to Mr. Kordic's best nature, to allow the evacuation of these children. Mr. Kordic replied dismissively with the words to the effect of, "If these two Muslim children are so important to you, you can have them," with which everybody sat down to lunch. And my Liaison Officer arranged their evacuation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel Williams, the date of 21st February, was there any particular international agreement that was to be undertaken around that time or slightly afterward?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As I stated, on the 23rd of February a ceasefire agreement was signed in Zagreb, which then came into effect on the 25th of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And was the Washington Accord discussed at all in any of these discussions that you and the International Community members had with the HVO and the Muslim group?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: To be honest, at the time, from our, perhaps, rather local perspective, a ceasefire was the most important thing we were looking for. And there had been many talks in Washington, Geneva and elsewhere, that this was a concrete military target that we were hoping for, which was a ceasefire. And so our focus tended to be on the ceasefire agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: However, this did predate the Washington Agreement by not too much time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The ceasefire came into effect, I think, just over two weeks before the actual political agreement was made.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And that agreement, effectively, put together the Muslim-Croat federation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just let me take a minute to make sure I've missed nothing. Looking at Z1349.1, dated 5 January. On page 3, under "Busovaca," there is a comment concerning the status of Kordic. Would you be able to comment on that comment?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The document describes Mr. Kordic as Colonel Kordic, a Vice-President of the HVO government/HDZ representative. I would simply say that I -- during my time, Mr. Kordic was never called Colonel Kordic in my presence, nor indeed did he call himself Colonel Kordic. I knew him then as I know him now, as Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you become aware of his acquiring another role under Ante Roso?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I've always assumed, as my predecessor Colonel Duncan had described him, that Mr. Kordic was a Vice-President of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and I was at no time privy to the internal mechanisms or structures of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and who filled which particular roles.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning your attention to page -- I'm sorry, to document 1366.2, which is from 9 February. Again, this whole month being a period leading up to the Washington Agreement. There is a comment about Mate Boban. Do you have any particular observations about this comment?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No. This is simply information that had clearly been passed to the Vitez LO by a Croat informant to one sort of another, official or unofficial. There's no mention of who had told Vitez LO that Mr. Boban had resigned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: After you left your tour of duty with the Coldstream Guards, did you ever meet Dario Kordic again, and if so, in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did meet Mr. Kordic one more time in the summer of 1995, I think in June, when I was the Deputy Chief U.N. military observer based in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what was the occasion?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The occasion was a religious festival in the town of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What role did Mr. Kordic play?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic was playing a leading role. He was, as it were, the chief host at this festival, which started with an open-air Catholic Mass and was then carried on with a supper party for an international political grouping which Mr. Carter, the former Civil Affairs Officer, was part of, and I was a guest of Mr. Carter on this evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was Mr. Kordic in a military attire at the time or how was he dressed, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic was very smartly dressed in a suit and was clearly enjoying the role of being a local political -- or the local political leader.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you recall if he was accompanied by any other persons from the government of Herceg-Bosna at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He was accompanied by a gentleman whom I had known from military commission meetings in Gornji Vakuf, who I believe was Mr. Djukic, who I knew as the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna Minister for Normalisation. I'm not sure what his proper title was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think I have covered the points that I wished to cover. There is one amplification I might ask about. In the use of airpower, are you aware of any offensive use of helicopters or fixed wing in the dropping of any munitions in the Bosnian territory for offensive use?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There were certainly two incidents. One when a 250-kilogramme bomb was dropped in an area to the south of the Vitez pocket. This was disarmed by my explosives officer. It had allegedly been dropped from a helicopter. There was no obvious military target in the area, so it was hard to see why this large munition had suddenly appeared from the sky, but it had undoubtedly arrived during our tour there and had buried itself some depth and had to be dug out and defused. On one other occasion, aerially delivered KB2 bomblets, these are small bombs, had been dropped in an area, Bosnian army held area around the Vitez pocket. Whether this was by helicopter or by aircraft, it was impossible for us to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The balance for the Court's -- for the balance of the documents which are labelled for admission, I will not discuss in any more detail. They are relevant in that they occurred during the time of the witness, and they had to be passed under his nose. There is one ECMM document that confirms information contained in a milinfosum. It simply is duplicative. I have been asked to bring to the Court's attention, by Ms. Verhaag, that we need a little guidance on the use of or the video insofar as the Defence is concerned. Would the Court permit us, would the Chamber permit us to offer the transcript only in light of the restrictions that ITN has placed on copying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want to have a look at this video, Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour. It seems to me to be a peripheral point, and we're perfectly happy if the Prosecution just puts a transcript in and substitutes it for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's part of a news broadcast and speaks for itself. Very well, the transcript can be put in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There are no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it would be a convenient moment. We'll adjourn now. Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. My name is Stephen Sayers. I'm one of the attorneys representing Dario Kordic. Behind me is Mr. Mikulicic, and he represents the other accused, Mario Cerkez. Sir, I'd just like to go into a few general areas of questions, and then -- and I'll indicate to you when we'll take up the story chronologically and just go through each of the meetings that you had with Mr. Kordic and others, and I apologise in advance for being a bit higgledy-piggledy with documents, but we received a large quantity of documents only this morning and I've had very little time to look through them. On the subject of documents, let me start with the report that you prepared. On the 22nd of September, 1994 -- the translators already have a copy of this. I'd just like to have you identify this document and confirm that it is the report concerning your tour in Central Bosnia, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document will be marked D166/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel, the document that's before you is, I believe, what I alluded to, a summary or report that you prepared for presentation to the Army Staff College at Camberley on September the 22nd, 1994, and it concerns basically the tour of duty of the 1st Battalion of the Coldstream Guards under your command from November 1993 until May of 1994. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I had prepared a long series of questions based upon this, but the document says what it says, and there appears to be very little point in going through to recite that. Suffice it to say I'd like to highlight just a few areas and move on smartly, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The second document, Colonel, that we received, it looks like it was extracts prepared from a contemporaneous diary that you maintained. This was turned over to us this morning, and I'd just like to have you identify this, if I may. Thank you. And the translators also have a copy of this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document will be marked D167/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel, this appears to be extracts from a diary that you maintained regarding the significant defence under your command, and that it appears to have been typed up at some subsequent time; is that correct to say?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Just one matter of detail, Colonel. Do you actually speak Croatian yourself?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You've also been shown a number of milinfosums, or military information summaries or intelligence summaries, Colonel. Would it be fair to say that these are reliable, contemporaneous summaries of all of the significant occurrences, events or meetings in your regiment's area of responsibility, and that they were prepared by experienced and capable intelligence officers under your command?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And these gentlemen, to use the vernacular, were trained professionally, to separate out the wheat from the chaff, if you like?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I would describe some of the factual points in them are as they had picked up the information. Some of the comments, particularly with hindsight, perhaps, were not all that they might be, but they were the best attempt that was available at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. It would be fair to say, and I don't think there is any dispute on this, that these military intelligence summaries basically present an evolving picture of your understanding of relationships on the ground, command relationships, political occurrences, things of that variety, significant events in your area of responsibility. Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They are indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, with respect to the diaries that we've had marked as an exhibit, and which you've identified. I believe, and it actually says it right on the front page, that you received some advice from Colonel Stewart to ensure that you kept a contemporaneous diary, so that you could keep track of things, what people were saying, who you met, things of that variety; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, indeed, you yourself refer in your September report, on page 2, to this diary as a reference document. And that's how you used it, and that's what you intended, as you were keeping the entries in a contemporaneous fashion? Would that be fair to say too?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was an attempt to, at the end of the day, to sum up the things that appeared to have been important during the course of the day. I would not claim that it contains everything that occurred, just things that struck me late at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But it is, nonetheless, the most contemporaneous source of information about the meetings that you had with Mr. Kordic, for example, that we have? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Along with the report of the 16th of November, which is a contemporaneous report of -- made by the Liaison Officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And would you agree that there were no other contemporaneous reports of the type that you've just referred to? And I don't have the reference ready to hand, but it was a November the 16th report prepared by your Liaison Officer for Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was, indeed, prepared by the Liaison Officer. And it is unusual, as far as I am aware, in existing. Thereafter, our meetings tended not to result in minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I put my fingers on it, and it is Exhibit Z1305.4. It looks like the Busovaca Liaison Officer was Captain Graham; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I take it, sir, that Captain Graham sat in on your meetings of November 16th, 1993 with Mr. Kordic, and presumably prepared notes himself, which ultimately were reduced to written form in this report?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There are no other reports of this type concerning your meetings with Mr. Kordic in December and February, I take it, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I am not aware of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one very brief question on this particular point, sir. At the time that you took over command of the UNPROFOR component that you've identified as Operation Grapple 3, your predecessor was Lieutenant-Colonel Duncan, conducting Operation Grapple 2 under the -- he was the Commander of Prince of Wales Own Regiment of Yorkshire; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that he had a difficult relationship with the Croats, as a result of his regiment having shot to death quite a few Croats during the course of his tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have no idea what his battalion had done. For example, I have never seen a post-tour report by his battalion, so I can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever seen an article published in The Guardian on April 2nd, 1996, referring to the Prince of Wales Own Regiment of Yorkshire, as SheetBat, a moniker that they had earned as a result of what I just referred to, the many shootings of Croats during the tour of duty of the POW?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did in fact see that article. It, I felt, covered a period wider than that of the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment, and I was -- I frankly thought it was unbalanced, when viewed in terms of my own battalion's performance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one question on your own chain of command, Colonel. And you've referred to this on page 6 and 7 of your report, your report of September the 22nd, 1994. What you wrote is fairly self-evident, but would it be fair to say that other components of UNPROFOR, other national contingents, found the chain of command within BritBat to be rather confusing?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, I believe that you had troops affiliated with the British Army operating in your area, to be specific, sappers, medics and logistics troops, who did not actually fall under your command, but rather came under the command of ComBrit 4 in Split. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Indeed, you make a comment on page 7, that if this situation seemed bizarre, to you yourself at BritBat, it was incomprehensible to other U.N. Contingents and led to many misunderstandings. And that's still your view today, is it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's regrettably true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn to the general military situation that confronted you, as you took over command, sir. On page 14 and 24 of your September the 22nd, 1994 report, you say that you found yourself or your soldiers embroiled in the middle of a vicious civil war or a full-blown civil war, as you call it on page 24. Would it be fair to say that in early November, as your troops assumed their duties, the Muslim forces had just created a complete -- completed rather, a successful series of co-ordinated offensives throughout Central Bosnia, mounted in Travnik, Kakanj, Bugogno, Fojnica, and just before you started your duties, Vares on November the 2nd, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't feel competent, I'm afraid, to comment on what had happened before I got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well, sir. Then I will move on. You have made comment in your September, 1994, report on pages 8 and 16 to the complexity of the front lines that you were called upon, if you like, to monitor and deal with. It would be fair to say that this was indeed a complex situation, with occasionally front lines running through the middle of the town, such as Vitez and Novi Travnik, and occasionally you find Muslim enclaves within Croat enclaves surrounded by hostile forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think that's a fair description.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You found that a very complex ongoing situation with which to deal with; would that be fair to say, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And indeed this led to sort of hyper precise, if you like, attempts to describe the situation of the citizens of Stari Vitez, for example. And you refer to this on page 16 of your report, an attempt to try to work out some language between both of the warring factions that described the situations of the citizens of Stari Vitez. You say that the ultimate decision was to refer to it as the area occupied by the Bosnian army inside the area occupied by the Croatian Defence Forces. Do you recall that comment, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do. At the time, both parties wished to conclude the agreement, but were finding it difficult to find a form of words that was acceptable to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So that elliptical but descriptive terminology was what was ultimately agreed upon by both parties, I take it?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a few more general questions along these lines, sir. Would it be fair to say that during this civil war, you found a general atmosphere of lawlessness and danger that prevailed, to a greater extent in areas controlled by the Muslim forces, and to a lesser extent in the Croat enclaves?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was undoubtedly danger in all areas. As I've stated earlier this morning, the area under the command of -- under the control of the Croat authorities generally was of a more peaceful character internally, although the front lines were obviously dangerous on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall receiving reports in January of 1994, from the Chief of Civil Police in Zenica, Mr. Mirsad Pajic, to the effect that the crime rate in Zenica had increased tenfold since before the war?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't remember receiving such a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That would not be inaccurate, though, would it?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have no idea. I don't have any idea of the statistics of crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. I have, sir, a number of military intelligence reports that I would like to go over with you, as we proceed chronologically through the time that you spent in Central Bosnia during your first tour. Let me just show you one of them, milinfosum number 1, dated November the 1st, 1993. I wonder, Mr. President, if we might have page 1 of this document put on the ELMO for the translators since I had not provided a copy of this to them previously.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D168/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel, had the Coldstream Guards actually assumed their duties by this time, November the 1st, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No we had not, but we had received military information responsibility, so this was the first milinfosum produced by my military information officer in his cell, but I did not arrive to take over formally about the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The 8th of November?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: 8th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. There is a reference in paragraph 3 to Mr. Neso Hurem, the Battalion Commander of the 325th Brigade, stating that the main BiH effort was still the Vitez pocket and there's a reference to sighting a number of Mujahedin to be loading various types of weaponry including, under item A there, 2 20-millimetre AAMGs. And I take it that stands for anti-aircraft machine gun?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And that's a 20-millimetre cannon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And the observation is made or the comment is made that this represents a sizeable increase in the amount of firepower into that area. Did you yourself ever see Mujahedin operating in the area of Kruscica or areas to the south of Vitez, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, I not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There is also a comment to a possible roulement of the 7th Muslim Brigade troops occurring in the village of Poculica. Two questions. Could you just tell me what a roulement is and what the 7th Muslim Brigade was, as far as you know, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
