utterances.text: The roulement is a military expression meaning a change from unit being replaced by another unit. And the 7th Muslim Brigade was an organisation within -- working within the 3rd Corps of the Bosnian Army. Most of its members were of a religious persuasion and most were displaced persons, as far as I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if you could just turn to page 3, under paragraph 11. You may have no detailed factual knowledge of this, but it seems to be motif for the times, if you like, the unfortunate times. There's a reference to seven people, and it appears to be Croats, who had been double crossed by Muslims and shot dead, having paid some 2,000 Deutschemarks apiece to be moved out of the area. Apparently they were all found shot in the head by pistol shots. Were you ever aware of that incident, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Other than having read this report, I have nothing that would confirm or deny the accuracy of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I -- would it be fair to say, sir, that even though, as terrible as this particular incident is, this would not be unusual of what was going on in Central Bosnia during the time that the Coldstream Guards were serving there from November 1993 to May of 1994, on both sides?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't think this incident, if it indeed occurred, could be seen as a typical incident. It would be a serious incident at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, sir. Indeed, another incident that's perhaps indicative of the deplorable times occurred in January of 1994, when a British citizen, Mr. Paul Goodall, a member of the Overseas Development Association, was murdered by Islamic gang in Zenica in late January of 1994. Do you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I remember the incident well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether any investigation was ever performed into that incident by the--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know, we've had, in the last 10 months, a deal of evidence about these sort of atrocities. I really wonder, Mr. Sayers, how this is going to help us decide the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I take your point, Mr. President, and I'm going to move on immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn to the situation of people in Stari Vitez, sir. You say that there were approximately 1,200 defenders in that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: One thousand two hundred inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Okay. I was just referring to page 4 of your September the 9th, 1994 report, but I think you've clarified that. Colonel Blaskic actually told your regiment that he was not opposed to allowing BritBat access to Stari Vitez in principle, but he was not prepared to risk the lives of his own troops in facilitating that access. Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's probably true. I would say that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And indeed that's reflected in a milinfosum, but since we've already covered that there's no point in going into that. Would it also be fair to say that this was significant sniper activity directed from Stari Vitez towards HVO Croat positions elsewhere in Vitez, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I would say that there was significant sniping activity by both sides, both into and out of Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And it would be fair to say as well, would it not, that the ABiH artillery resources on the high ground regularly shelled Vitez and they also regularly shelled Busovaca too, would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I would hesitate to use the word "regularly." The artillery assets available to the 3rd Bosnian Corps were limited, extremely limited, but I expect the bombardment was dependent on the availability of ammunition, which was somewhat infrequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And one last question about Stari Vitez. Did you ever meet (redacted)

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was not aware there was anyone qualified as a doctor in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On the subject of artillery, sir, I'd just like to show you one milinfosum generated by your military intelligence unit. It's milinfosum number 77 dated January the 16th, 1994. If you could put one -- page 1 on the ELMO, that would be useful. Just two brief questions in connection with this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D169/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Two things, sir. In connection with the observation made in paragraph 3 regarding BiH probing patrols being engaged by the HVO, it's true, is it not, that throughout your tour of duty, the Muslim objective was to cut or obtain control of the Vitez pocket, and that, in fact, two significant offensives attempted to achieve precisely that objective, one just before Christmas in 1993, and the other on January 9th, 1994?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not absolutely sure what the intention was, but certainty it appeared on the ground as if the intention was to cut the pocket in half, and I presume they assumed that the pocket would fall once it had been cut into two distinct pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, in fact, you are in experience, sir, with the Soviet Bloc military tactics, slicing of pockets up into smaller pockets is relatively standard strategic and tactical doctrine, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This was a -- I don't think anybody else's doctrine was involved in this. This was the narrowest point. This was the neck of the pocket. It was the most obvious place to attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And by "this," just so that the record is clear, you're referring to the narrowest of the Vitez-Busovaca pocket at the area of Santici, on the main supply route; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The second question, sir, in paragraph 4, your liaison officer reported that there was a relatively high level of artillery and mortar activity into Vitez and that the observation made was this appears to be harassment fire on the town to maintain the pressure on the HVO. Do you know whether any militaries targets were being targeted by this harassment fire or was it just fire launched generally into the area of Vitez where people were living and working?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the actual details or indeed what is meant by "relatively high," but in comparison to artillery levels, each of the artillery into the Gornji Vakuf area, for example, artillery fire into the Vitez area was of a minimal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to Gornji Vakuf, sir, is it true that the HVO attempted to avoid hitting the BritBat base or U.N. convoys during periods of active fighting and you were, in fact, informed of that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, this is true, both in the case of Gornji Vakuf and, I believe, in the case of the Vitez area as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You never heard of Mr. Kordic ever appearing in the Gornji Vakuf area, did you, sir? Ever being present in that area?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was not aware of him being in that area at all, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, and we'll get into this just a second, as I understand, Gornji Vakuf fell within a completely different command zone of the HVO from the Vitez-Busovaca pocket --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must first of all establish whether the witness knows about the HVO command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Colonel, do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I know a certain amount, Your Honour. I wouldn't claim to be a great expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The Presiding Judge points out very correctly that I have to establish that you know something about it, but before I can answer [sic] a question of detail like that. Were you aware that the military chain of command had its pinnacle, if you like, at the general staff in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the Commander In Chief during your tour of duty, sir, I believe you've identified him as Lieutenant General Ante Roso.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I met General Roso.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He was the Commander In Chief of the HVO Armed Forces throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct. As far as I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in addition, sir, would it be fair to say that the organisation of the HVO forces was arranged into various so-called Operative Zones with, I believe, the north-west Herzegovina Operative Zone, including Gornji Vakuf, being under the command of Brigadier Skender, I believe?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As far as I was aware, the area of Prozor area that we're talking about to the south of Gornji Vakuf came under Tomislavgrad in -- overall but its forward headquarters in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And do you know who the Zone Commander was in that zone, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I met two people in Gornji -- Prozor. One was Colonel Siljeg, and he was then replaced by Colonel Skender.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And no one ever mentioned that -- Mr. Kordic's name during the times that you were meeting with Brigadier Skender or Colonel Siljeg, did they?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't recall his name being mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In each Operative Zone, sir, and let's turn specifically to the Central Bosnia Operative Zone about which I would venture to say you know most, would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Within each Operative Zone, there were a municipality-based brigades, each with their own Commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And those Brigade Commanders would in turn report up the chain of command to the Operative Zone Command near your zone, being Colonel Tihomir Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that the -- well, do you know who the Commander of the brigade in Busovaca was?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just show you two milinfosums, the first being milinfosum number 5, dated November the 5th, 1993, and the second being milinfosum 8, dated November the 8th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The milinfosum of the 5th of November will be marked D170/1, and the one of 8 November D171/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Once again very brief questions on this, Colonel. Turning to the first document, the milinfosum number 5, would you just look at page 2, paragraph 10? There's a reference there to Dusko Grubesic, Commander Nikola Subic-Zrinjski HVO Brigade. Were you ever able to interact yourself with the Busovaca Brigade Commander, Commander Gubesic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I take it, sir, that contacts between your soldiers and the Bigade Commander at the local level would have occurred at the level of a Liaison Officer and not at the Commander's level, not at your level?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It would have been either a Company Commander or more likely the Liaison Officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And secondly, sir, milinfosum number 8 on page 2, paragraph 10, refers to military predictions made by Commander Gubesic to your Busovaca Liaison Officer, fearing that his troops on the ground or fearing that the next offensive would be against the Vitez pocket and reporting that the HVO appeared to be somewhat resigned to that perception. Were you aware of that perception on the part of the HVO, that they perceived that the Vitez pocket would be the target of the next BiH offensive?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think, viewed from a perspective of a local commander like Mr. Grubesic, it was a very fair assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Just one question on Lieutenant-General Roso. You were aware, were you not, that he actually spent 20 years serving in the French Foreign Legion?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I knew that, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, turning to Colonel Blaskic for just a minute. He was the, as you've said, the Commander of the Operative Zone and was, in fact, the Military Commander of all Armed Forces on the Croat side in Central Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As it would appear through the military chain of command, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You never saw anything to lead you to a different conclusion, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As I stated earlier on, my view is that, when in the presence of Mr. Kordic, Colonel Blaskic always deferred to him as if Mr. Kordic was in charge, and indeed we always viewed Mr. Kordic as the man who could deliver. Whereas Blaskic could quite often just say that something was impossible, Mr. Kordic would always tell you why -- the policy was for it to be impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Just give the interpreters, Colonel, a chance to catch up. Colonel Blaskic, to your knowledge, was in fact a professional military Officer, having obtained an Officer's rank in the JNA before the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He was a young Officer before the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would agree, sir, that military Officers are normally respectful in the presence of senior political figures; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This is quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, sir, I'm sure that you yourself are very respectful when you receive visits from members of parliament or members of the government? Would that be fair to say? But that certainly doesn't mean, sir, that Members of Parliament or Members of the Government can issue a direct military order to you, does it?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The Members of the Parliament or, rather, Ministers are the people who determine the policy that soldiers shall carry out. We don't determine policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Certainly, sir, as part of the government, but as individuals they don't have the power to issue military orders to you. That's the only point that I am getting at.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The point that I am making is that we take our orders from Ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Blaskic never told you on any occasion that he had to obey orders from Mr. Kordic, did he, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Not in so many words, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There is no reference to it in your diary, or any milinfosum. And I think that it would be fair to say that there is no report, of which you are aware, prepared by your battalion which contains any reference to the fact that Colonel Blaskic had to defer to orders given to him by Mr. Kordic? Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think the reports make it clear, in so many words, that we assumed that Mr. Kordic was in charge, and that Mr. Kordic also assumed that he was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Well, we've established that you never asked Colonel Blaskic the question. Did you ever ask Mr. Kordic whether he had the power or authority, actually, to issue military orders, for example?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic often said that he would make things possible. As I say, he had the ability, in the view of myself and other members of the International Community, to make things happen. Now, these things were either -- were not purely military, perhaps they were to do with relations with the International Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But did you ever ask a question, did he have the ability to give military orders? Did you ever clear that issue up?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Not in so many words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Quite apart from Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic, did you ever ask Colonel Filipovic, for example, whether Mr. Kordic had any military authority, or, for that matter, any other Bosnian Croat Military Commander or political figure?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Colonel Filipovic was, I would say, too busy fighting a war to be willing to take time out to make political comments like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would the answer to the question then be no?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The answer would be no, I had no conversation with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me, Colonel, proceed chronologically through your tour of duty. The next milinfosum I would like you to look at is milinfosum number 13, dated November 13, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D172/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One brief question on this, Colonel. It's on page 2, paragraph 9. There is a reference to a meeting between the Zenica Liaison Officer, a meeting with Dzemal Merdan, the Deputy Commander of the 3rd Corps, and a response to a request made by Colonel Blaskic for safe passage to attend his father's funeral in Kiseljak. Do you recall that this request was turned down by Dzemal Merdan?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: My only recollection is what I see here in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection, independent of this report, sir, or does this accurately encapsulate the state of the Coldstream Guards knowledge as of this date on that particular subject?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This is clearly the view, as put by Colonel Merdan, as to why he believed Colonel Blaskic really wanted to go to Kiseljak. I have no reason to have an opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked some questions in connection with threats to explode the Vitezit factory. I do not have any questions for you on that subject, other than this one: It's fair to say that this was a -- was a sort of an old story, if you like; threats to explode the factory had been made for a number of months, even before your regiment assumed their duties? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, they went back some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you had occasion, did you not, to exchange many pieces of correspondence back and forth with Colonel Blaskic and the HVO headquarters in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I believe that on February the 22nd, 1994, you wrote a letter thanking Colonel Blaskic and the HVO for co-operation extended to BritBat during the Muslim offensive in late December, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Indeed, sir, that offensive involved one particular incident involving the deaths of 60 or 70 Croats at Krizancevo Selo. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Notwithstanding the fact that the Croats in the pocket, the Vitez pocket, were under assault, they permitted United Nations convoys to use alternative routes through the Vitez area, when the main road, the main supply route itself, was under a sustained ABiH attack; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And then one other letter that you wrote to Colonel Blaskic was congratulating him on his appointment to the HVO general staff in Mostar, I believe in March or May of 1994. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know who promoted him?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, I had only heard as a rumour that he had been promoted, I think through the world service or some such thing. And so I took the opportunity to write to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know who made promotion decisions within the HVO, or the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You touched lightly on this, and I'll touch equally lightly, Colonel. Would it be fair to say that you did not undertake any significant effort to obtain information on Bosnian Croat political institutions, and most particularly, the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: My dealings with the Croatian or the Croat authorities were purely linked to trying to deliver humanitarian aid and fulfil my mission. It went no further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. You didn't perform any study of the members of the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna or the political institutions that were set up when that entity was established on the 28th of August of 1993? Would that be fair to say as well?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I never tasked my military information cell to produce anything like that, and we never saw anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Turning to your meetings with Mr. Kordic, Colonel. I think I counted, from the papers, five meetings. You've described one on November the 16th of 1993. There was another one that you described on December the 1st of 1993. There was -- yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There was a meeting that you described on February 3rd, 1993. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There is one that you didn't describe, but is referred to in a milinfosum on February the 9th, I'll show you that. The final meeting you had with Mr. Kordic, before the war's end, was February the 21st, 1993. And you've described that; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then -- sorry, just to complete it. You had one other meeting with him, about a year after the end of the war, a year or so, in the summer of 1995, and you described that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, it's true that, in your view, he was the political leader of Croats in the Lasva Valley; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And I think that you've referred, on November the 16th, February the 8th, and February the 9th, in your diary to that and, just for the Trial Chamber's reference, that can be found at pages 3, 18 and 19. On page 10 of the statement that you gave to the Prosecution in June of 1998, sir, you said that you never, in fact, saw Mr. Kordic in full military uniform, and never heard him referred to as anything other than Mr. Kordic. Is that still --

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I would say that the second part, indeed, I never heard him referred to as anything else than Mr. Kordic. I never saw him -- when I say full military uniform, I never saw him wear a badge of rank or, indeed, wear a military head dress, but I did see him wear camouflage clothing and, on this one occasion, the 16th of November, he was wearing an HVO arm patch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Were you aware that Mr. Kordic actually gave weekly press conferences in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. They are mentioned occasionally in the milinfosums.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, indeed, when you first met Mr. Kordic, it was your understanding that he was the vice-president of the HDZ party; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's what I've been led to believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, in fact, sir, that was true, wasn't it? As far as you know, he was, in fact, one of the five vice-presidents of the HDZ, BiH, the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I believed it to be true, that he was a vice-president. I can't say how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you may not know the answer to this, sir, but do you know who the President of that political party was, at the time that you were in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I assume that Mr. Boban was the President at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn to the November the 16th meeting. You say that Mr. Kordic was dressed in a camouflage waistcoat, that he didn't wear any military insignia or rank badges; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, he was wearing a camouflage waistcoat. Yes, he was not wearing any military badges of rank, but he was wearing an HVO arm patch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This was the only time that you saw him wear that patch, though, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's the only time that I can confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if we could show -- if you could just refer to Exhibit Z1305.2, which I think is the milinfosum which describes this particular meeting, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If you could just turn to page 2. There is a reference to the fact that the Commanding Officer of BritBat visits Mr. Kordic, and that certain freedom of movement issues are discussed. And the comment is made that: "Mr Kordic's authority over the military commanders in the area is in question. The immediate future may provide answers to who holds real power in the area." Do you know whose commentary that was?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's not my commentary. It's the commentary of the military information cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was that comment based, in any way, upon briefings that you gave to your military intelligence cell following the conclusion of this meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And as we go through your contemporaneous diary, sir, on page 3. The entry under the 16th of November is rather brief, I think you'll agree. And it says: "The commanding officer visited Dario Kordic, HVO political leader, and member of the government of the so-called Croat republic of Herceg-Bosna and his lair just south of Busovaca." What did you mean by liar?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic was living, I believe it's called Tisovac, to the south of Busovaca, but it was down a mountain road and very much at the end of the world. It did seem rather like a wolf's lair in some ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that you viewed Mr. Kordic early on as someone who had the status of a war criminal?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I've reached that conclusion early on. It was only after my -- some of my dealings with him that led me to believe that he was not, perhaps, a very compassionate person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If we take a look at page 6 of your diary, you refer to a meeting on December the 1st, where you say that: "Kordic refused all Stari Vitez casevacs, except to the Croat Nova Bila hospital, until Croat casevacs could travel to Kiseljak. Characteristic bloody-mindedness (he was later indicted as a war criminal, and rightly so.)" The casevac, does that refer to casualty evacuation?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: These are civilian casualty evacuations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When did you add that comment, sir, to your diary?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's when I put the comments together in 19 -- as per the end. 1995, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Proceeding chronologically, sir. The next item that I have a note of is you were asked about the identity of a person named Chris Wilson. I would just like to show you the next milinfosum number 17. And that's already been marked I believe as Z1308.1. In paragraph 3, on the first page of this document, there is a reference to this person, Chris Wilson. And the intelligence report says that he has gone to some lengths to conceal his identity from BritBat and is reported to be a former member of Operation Grapple 1. Operation Grapple 1, I take it, sir, was the operation that was run under the auspices of the Cheshire Regiment commanded by Colonel Stewart; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right did you ever receive information to the effect that this apparently English soldier was affiliated in any way with a group known as the Jokers?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I know nothing more about this Chris Wilson than what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. The next item, chronologically, Colonel, is a reference that you made to an agreement signed in Geneva on November the 29th, 1993. It's true, is it not, that this agreement was signed by the commander of all of UNPROFOR forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, General Cot?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And negotiated between General Rasim Delic, the Commander of the Forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And for the HVO General Milivoj Petkovic, the Chief Of Staff under General Ante Roso, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Kordic was not involved in any of those negotiations, was he, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that it was your practice to require your soldiers to keep a copy of this agreement in their vehicles as they tried to pass through checkpoints; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that was because one of the points agreed upon at the Geneva conference was a guarantee of freedom of movement to international agencies; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Generally speaking, would it be fair to say that you encountered few, if any, restrictions on movement in the Vitez-Busovaca pocket --

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Those --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- this agreement?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: After this agreement. I don't believe, to be quite honest, that the agreement made any great difference. There were restrictions that were imposed by either side, by either the Muslims or the Croats, were, I believe, largely to do with the primacy of the war effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's true, it is not, sir, that Colonel Blaskic actually notified BritBat in writing that all checkpoints in the Vitez-Busovaca pocket would be closed from dusk to dawn and that he notified BritBat of that after the Geneva agreement?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And, in fact, I think you found this to be a fairly sensible arrangement, consistent with safety and the practice insofar as UNHCR convoys were concerned anyway, which was not to run those convoys at night?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The principle was that white vehicles become black in the dark and are, therefore, fair game.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, therefore, you did not disagree with that directive issued by Colonel Blaskic, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We did not disagree with it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Colonel, that brings us to the December the 1st, 1993 meeting that you had with Mr. Kordic, and I believe that in response to the arguments that you made, in your view Mr. Kordic came up with political arguments to articulate the Croat position with respect to the arguments that you were making; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I described earlier, yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Looking at your diary, there's no reference to the particular content of any discussions that you had with Mr. Kordic on that date, or insofar as they related to casevacs. Let me just ask you one question, sir. You said that Mr. Kordic said something about crossing a border. Are you sure that he said an international border?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm absolutely positive. My memory of it is it was a particularly remarkable statement and that's why it stuck in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that the Stoltenberg-Owen Plan actually envisaged an arrangement to forge a peace in Central Bosnia, and that arrangement involved the establishment of three separate constituent republics, ethnically based republics within the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There were many plans. I don't feel that they were relevant to the situation at the time. I was dealing with the situation on the 1st of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were aware, though, that the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna had already been established at that time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was aware that there was an organisation going by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And were you aware that that was set up in the same month as the Stoltenberg-Owen Plan was actually approved?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't be able to put the two events together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So suffice it to say, sir, that you weren't -- you did not yourself undertake any study of the relationship between the timing of the establishment of the HR H-B, the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and the details of the Stoltenberg-Owen Plan; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That doesn't really matter. The issue is: Did Mr. Kordic say that it would involve crossing an international border? I take it, from what you're saying, that that is challenged; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. That -- that is challenged. I think that the discussion -- the Defence's position, if I may articulate it, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, no. It's merely matter of whether the comment is challenged or not, whatever the plans may have said at the time. The witness's evidence is that Mr. Kordic said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Quite so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Are you sure that that was the precise translation that was given to you of the observation made by Mr. Kordic, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As I have said, it was such a remarkable statement that it stuck in my mind and chilled me to the point where I could go no further with the argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. And it would also be fair to say that you did not make any contemporaneous note of that comment or report it to your military intelligence cell; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It does not appear in the military information summary, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You didn't make a note of it in your diary either, did you?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I can't say yes or no to that, as I don't have -- this is a summary of my diaries. I don't have them available to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. Moving on. Towards the end of 1993, there is a reference in your diary to attacks launched against the Vitez-Busovaca pocket on December the 22nd and 24th of 1993. It's on page 9. On December the 22nd, the BiH launched -- offensives launched in the Vitez pocket and in the Gornji Vakuf area. There's also a reference to 60 or 70 HVO being killed by a surprise attack at Krizancevo Selo near Dubravica. Would it be fair to say, sir, that that event involving so many deaths raised some particularly hard feelings on the part of the Croats battling for their lives against this sustained assault?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Indeed. There were immediate allegations that this was a massacre, and we followed this up later on, early in the new year, to investigate the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just digress for one instant and raise the subject that you alluded to in your direct testimony, sir, regarding aid convoys and attacks launched upon aid convoys. Would it be fair to say that there was a general problem of banditry plaguing aid deliveries to needy areas during the -- during the war?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was a problem of banditry. Banditry is one of a number of problems. Banditry in itself was, I would say, almost uniquely a -- the problem of Muslim areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And there was actually an incident in February of 1994, February the 14th, I believe, when about 15 tonnes of aid were stolen from the Novi Travnik area, and the Muslim military police just looked on while this looting was going on and did absolutely nothing about it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And would it also be fair to say, sir, that the problems of banditry, insofar as to aid convoys were concerned, actually inside the Busovaca pocket, had pretty much been brought under control by the HVO Military Police during the time that you were in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do not recall any instances, what I would describe as banditry within the Vitez Croat-controlled area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Sir, the next item I would like to bring to your attention chronologically is the offensive that followed the Christmas offensive of 1993. It's true that a major offensive was launched against the narrow point in the Vitez-Busovaca pocket. That's Santici, as you've describe, on January the 9th, 1993, and that is described in your diary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. The military intelligence summary, sir, that I referred to on February the 9th, which is the next item that I'd like to cover with you, is milinfosum 101, and I would like you to take a look at that, if you would, and have it marked as the next exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If the registrar would put page 2 on the ELMO for the interpreters. At the bottom of the page is what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D173/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There is a reference in your diary, sir, on page 19 to a meeting with Dario Kordic, who is referred to as the HVO political leader in Central Bosnia. Do you have any recollection of this meeting or what was discussed at it?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't have any -- it doesn't strike me particularly as anything that I can add to what I've written in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's quite all right, Colonel. This was a long time ago. But the comment or the intelligence report is that Mr. Kordic was keen to point out that the HVO were doing all they could to avoid UNPROFOR during any fighting and was reported to be generally co-operative. Presumably that was a report from you, that you had found Mr. Kordic to be co-operative during this meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, he's saying that the HVO were being co-operative, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. In connection with the testimony that you gave that Mr. Kordic was somehow the Assistant Chief Of Staff to General Roso, were you aware that General Roso had actually been appointed to the Presidential Council to the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna to advise President Boban on strategic and other matters?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just so that my question is clear, you were not aware that he was actually a member of the government of the HR H-B as well as being the head of the military forces?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I knew him only as the leader of the military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. That brings us, Colonel, to the February 21st, 1994 meeting. It's described first in your contemporaneous diary at page 23, I believe. You refer to this as a great showdown with the HVO in the Vitez pocket, with a number of people being present, Mr. Kordic, Colonel Blaskic, Marinko Bosjnak, Mr. Rajic, and others. You also testified, sir, I think during direct, that you presented Mr. Kordic with the -- with a form letter that was to be distributed both to the Croat side and Muslim side in connection with a recent event; is that right? A protest letter.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Two protest letters but -- were different, but the aim was similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was the protest letter actually addressed specifically to Mr. Kordic? Let me just take a look at that if I may.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't think it's addressed specifically to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know whether Mr. Kordic had been given any advanced notice that this document was going to be laid upon him, if you like?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So it came as a surprise to him?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. The observation is made in your diary, sir, that after a tense period, all agreed to try harder and Kordic magnanimously agreed to two immediate casevacs being removed from LO Vitez by Stari Vitez. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And that represented your view contemporaneously recorded; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is an abbreviated view. As I explained earlier on, I first asked for these immediate casualty evacuations and was turned down. I have to say I got very upset about this, and that was when Sir Martin Garrod stepped in to try one more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Presumably he was a little calmer and the issue was quickly worked out, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Older and wiser, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But issue was, nonetheless, quickly worked out, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Relatively quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You did not prepare any other document other than what we see in your diary that reflects this conversation, did you?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the only other document of which I'm aware that refers to it is the milinfosum that has previously been marked as Z1383.1. I just wonder if you'd just put that in front of you, sir. Now, sir, looking at paragraph 4 on page 1, there's a report from your Liaison Officer. I take it that your Liaison Officer was present at this meeting too?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And Mr. Kordic was clearly the Chairman of the meeting, presiding over the meeting, with an important political figure present such as Sir Martin Garrod, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic was chairing the meeting, I think. I'm not sure whether Sir Martin Garrod's presence has any bearing on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And the observation is made by the Military Intelligence Officer that it is absolutely apparent that Colonel Blaskic was far better informed than Mr. Kordic on issues relating to the pocket. Is that consistent with your recollection, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I don't have a detailed recollection of that aspect. That is the view of the Liaison Officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So you can't help us one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Can't say -- I can't say he's wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And two days later, sir, there was a ceasefire agreement, as you've previously described, signed in Zagreb, and I believe that the signatories for the various warring factions once again were General Delic on the Muslim side and General Roso on the Croat side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Mr. Kordic wasn't involved in any of those negotiations, was he? Not as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Not as far as I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Final subject, sir. You never saw any HV troops or officers in the Vitez-Busovaca pocket at any time during your tour of duty, did you?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I never saw any, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. That concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. I appreciate your patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, bearing in mind that the witness spoke about the period of time covering from 11th -- from November 1993 onward and it doesn't cover the period for which my client, Mr. Cerkez, has been accused, so that the Defence of Mr. Cerkez has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just a couple of points, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Concerning, the use of the term "magnanimous" in your diary about Mr. Kordic's giving over the Muslim evacuees, what was the tone of that term? He magnanimously gave it over. I think it's on page 23 of the diary. February 21st entry.

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Indeed. My clear recollection of the event is that when Sir Martin Garrod entered the debate to try and persuade Mr. Kordic that he, in what I would describe as dismissive manner, stated, as I've said earlier, words to the effect of "Well, if these two Muslim children mean so much to you, then you can have them."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And there was a sarcastic tone, is that --

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it could be described as sarcastic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The attitude that was suggested that it was held by General Merdan about allowing Colonel Blaskic to travel, I'd just like to ask you to turn, if you can, to the milinfosum from 18 November. It is in the pile. Z1310.1, and in the interests of time I shall read out the passage. It's paragraph 4 under Vitez. It said: "The commanding officer visited Tihomir Blaskic, Commander, HVO, 3rd Operational Zone, Central Bosnia, today. When asked about the possibility of allowing aid through to Stari Vitez, he relied, 'Why should I give aid to my enemies?'" Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Indeed I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It was brought to your attention that Colonel Blaskic was promoted to the main staff of the HVO. Are you also aware that Colonel Blaskic was made by General -- by President Tudjman a General in the Croatian Army after he was indicted by this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I know -- I've read this in the newspaper since, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You have a background, Colonel, you indicated, in Soviet affairs insofar as military-style structures is concerned. Are you familiar with the term "political officer" or "Polit Officer" or Zam Polit"?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I am indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you comment on the nature of the authority that would be vested in a Political Officer?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Normally a Political Officer would be, although technically subordinate to the Commander, would, in fact, be giving him advice on political matters and effectively ensuring that party control was maintained.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And, in fact, was to -- had active intervention potential in any situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection to the leading nature of that question, and it's a little beyond the scope of direct examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you also aware, in connection with General Roso, that he was an HV Officer?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I am not aware where he came from. I knew that he had been in the Foreign Legion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Counsel opposite raised a question about the title or the role of Mr. Kordic as Assistant Chief Of Staff to General Roso. Turning your attention briefly to Exhibit -- it's actually an ECMM document that was given in connection with a previous exhibit, but it's Z1343, which is connected with, in terms of contents, Z1363.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I did not ask any questions about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I agree. Let's move on. Anything more?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think we pretty well covered --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Krizancevo Selo. You indicated that there was an investigation as to the allegations of massacre by the Croats -- Croats alleging massacre on the Croats. What conclusion was reached as to massacre?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The elaborate investigation was taken -- was conducted at the spot where 27 of the bodies of those who had allegedly been killed were buried. We exhumed nine bodies in the presence of the BBC, amongst other people. To the best of our limited knowledge, they all appeared to be of military age and to have died in extreme traumatic ways, that we assessed as being in combat. We then interviewed three men who had been captured, who were in the gaol in Zenica, and we eventually presented a report, not only to the U.N. authorities, but also to the Croat military authorities in the Vitez pocket.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Then did your investigation sustain the allegations by the Croats?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The investigation suggested that there was -- there was no evidence to support the theory of a massacre. The evidence pointed to a tactical success that had led to a considerable loss of life.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Had it ever been brought to your attention that there was implementation of a proposed plan called Owen-Stoltenberg?

utterances.speaker: PETER GAGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was not aware, until this was brought up a short time ago, of the details of the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Colonel that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are released.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was told by my learned friends this morning that they would be cross-examining into the middle of the afternoon, but time has gone more quickly for them. I told them there probably wasn't a witness available this afternoon. Sir Martin Garrod is here, but he's expressed a desire to familiarise himself with more of the documents than he was able to familiarise himself with yesterday. And although I'll have another word with him, it may be he would stick to his preference of not starting to give evidence until he's conducted a proper review, and it's probably his entitlement, in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The events took place six or seven years ago, so it seems to me that he is probably entitled to refresh his memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are some other matters that can be dealt with. Can I list them? First, there's another statement we wish to add, another witness we wish to call. I'll hand in his statement now, copies of it. If the usher would be so good. Served on my learned friends on Friday, as soon as we had it. I can deal with it all in due course later. I gather there is objection to it. It's a statement that deals with Stupni Do. It comes from, effectively, an insider. It unlocks the uncertainties about Stupni Do, if there were any. And the Court will find its particular value, not least in starting at paragraph 18. It may be that we could deal with that this afternoon, or it may be that will want a little more time to be dealt with. The Chamber will recall that the witness -- I think it's -- the Witness P in Blaskic. In any event, the diplomat style witness, whose transcript we wished to have read, but in respect of whom the Defence are seeking to have called. And that, I think, in light of earlier decisions, is something that has to be discussed. Either Defence have to explain why they want him called, to justify his being called, if he's prima facie a witness whose transcript from the other trial could or should be read. So that may be something we could conveniently deal with this afternoon. I can bring you up to date with the witness position. The Chamber will recall that the difficulties we face this week arise from the fact that Stutt has been denied us for the third time, I think, the second or third time, by reason of his important duties for the United Nations elsewhere. He's the witness I had considered dealing with by video-link, and although that would have involved members of your staff undergoing the hardship of travelling to New York, I was prepared to propose that, if it was otherwise realistic. But in light of both the volume of documents he'll have to deal with, which is very difficult via video, and in light of the fact that he's on a -- it's effectively been promised that he can be here on the 28th of February, I'm proposing to deal with him that way. But it's his absence this week that creates the slight difficulties that there are. I had a discussion with Mr. Stein last Friday about the witnesses producing the tape recording of Kordic and Blaskic. The Chamber may recall there was the possibility of their argument being dealt with without evidence. It seemed to me it was going to be very difficult for them not to want to have one of the witnesses here, especially if they are challenging the provenance of that tape. A suggestion was made by Mr. Stein that they could deal with the matter on paper, and just deal with the legality of the taking of the tape as an issue. I raised with him, "Well, if you are dealing with it on paper, does that mean that your are abandoning any arguments about the provenance of the tape?" And he said he wasn't. It seemed to me impossible, really, to leave matters on that unsatisfactory basis. So I am making efforts to have the witness, who deals with the provenance of the tape, available this week. I shall probably know at lunch time whether he is going to be available, before his deployment to the United States of America. So he may come as a witness to fill in. And that issue may be dealt with later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The argument for that point is listed for this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is listed for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But the Defence were going to let me know whether they required the witnesses to attend, and it was only when I saw their skeleton, or their latest summarised objection, that I could see that it might be very difficult for them to mount that argument without having and cross-examining the evidence itself. You can hardly challenge the provenance of a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Whatever the problems, we should stick to this timetable, because if we let matters slip, there will be a great deal to deal with at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely. The witness, in respect of whom a successful application was made to add to the list last week, is not available this week. He doesn't have travel documents. So I can't call him. And there is then outstanding the issue of those -- was it six witnesses who were listed as transcript witnesses in our latest amended overview of the indictment -- overview of witnesses, a separate list at the end of that document. We have yet to hear what the Defence attitude towards those transcript witnesses is. But that's something that might be dealt with this week as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We might be able to deal with that, at least, in a --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After lunch, there may be something to deal with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let me finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Defence should be ready at least to give us a preliminary idea this afternoon about the transcript witnesses. We can begin the discussion. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry to have interrupted you. I'll have another word with Sir Martin, because, obviously, if he is willing to press on, so much the better. The only other way of dealing with it, would be to take him through his evidence in chief, on the basis that, uniquely with him, we are able to continue discussing with him documents after the close of the Court this afternoon, for the production of further documents tomorrow. I don't particularly press that, but that's one way around the problem, if there are further documents to be reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am more than happy to let the Trial Chamber know what our position is with respect to the transcript witnesses, once I know who the transcript witnesses are. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The document was placed in their box on Friday, I having identified where they could find it earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. We'll resume this discussion after lunch. If we can deal with the witness, of course so much the better. But if not, there are obviously other matters which we can deal with. 2.35. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.05 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General Garrod would like to review his documents further, and indeed arrangements were made for him to leave the Tribunal and come back to complete that task a little later this afternoon. So he's not available, I'm afraid. I acted on the basis of the estimates of cross-examination that I was given. That leaves for determination this afternoon maybe some other matters. The witness statement I've just served is one to which, I gather, there is objection. I don't know if the Chamber has had an opportunity to look at it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us take that now, if you'd like to take a seat. You recommend paragraphs 18 onwards?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The whole of the document is of value and very considerable value, but certainly in order to save your time, I was going to invite you to go straight to paragraph 18 for what it reveals about Stupni Do. But, in fact, the whole of the document is of great value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we hear the Defence objection, Mr. Nice, it would be helpful to know how it comes that this arrives so late in the day here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. This witness was not known to the OTP prosecuting this case at all, save that it may be the case that his name appears simply as a name in a NordBat document, but it wasn't a NordBat document or statement which was in any way part of the Kordic or Blaskic set of papers. So he simply wasn't known to those prosecuting this case. A witness was called on the -- excuse my leaning down, but I think it was the 2nd of December of last year, and -- I'm just checking that he was -- well, let's assume that he was a protected witness, and I won't name him. He gave his evidence, and after he gave evidence and in the course of one of those informal discussions that I think I told you about last week, identified somebody who he then thought might be able to help us, and I think -- my recollection is that they were now neighbours, something to that effect, so that he had more recently had an opportunity to talk to him and told us that the man might be able to help us. I think I've said before, witnesses, when they're dealing with investigators or us in a formal basis, are themselves quite alert to the distinction of what they can say and what others can say and quite careful about that. In any case, he volunteered this name, a name not known to us before. It was given immediate top priority by us, or by me, and the witness was seen on a very preliminary basis on part of the mission to Bosnia that was already underway or planned and due to take place in a day or so. And we wrote to the Defence on the 14th of December, explaining to them that a witness who could help with Vares had been located and saying that indeed we hoped to be able to serve his statement before Christmas, and I made further arrangements that the witness might be seen by a local investigator. May we go into private session for just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Once seen, he was entirely co-operative, and although I've taken precautions in that last short passage to save his identity should he seek protective measures, he may be a witness who won't seek protective measures. I'm not sure about that. So those are the circumstances in which he came to our attention. There's no way we could have known of him before. And having known of him, not only have we done everything possible to obtain evidence from him, but I have done everything possible to alert the Defence to what would be likely to be coming, given that, of course, until he was seen, we certainly couldn't provide his name without his consent and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When would you propose to call him?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His movements remain somewhat difficult. He has indicated that he would be available at the end of February, 28th of February, and we have pressed him to hold that time available to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Preliminarily, we do not have the Croatian version of this statement available to review with our client, so I would like you to consider that in any ruling that you make. This statement was forwarded to us on Friday evening, January 28th. Over the weekend I reviewed it and was actually preparing an application to preclude his testimony, and having done that, I would like to file it with the Court now. As Your Honours can see from the front of the witness's statement, and this statement was taken on January 21 and 26 of this year, but if you turn to paragraph 33 of the witness's statement, you will see that as of 28 October, 1993, this witness was working with NordBat, one of the parts of the U.N. Protective Force in Bosnia, and indeed lived in their camp for the next six months, from October 1993 forward. Indeed, at paragraph 28 of his statement, he references giving documents to the NordBat Commander. The short version of our application and the short version for the reason we oppose this late entry is it's simply untimely. Mr. Nice's reference to the December 14th communication in which there was an oblique reference to a witness that may be called if they find someone, doesn't toll any responsibility or trigger any responsibility on our part to respond because there's nothing to respond to. I don't believe the Prosecutor has clearly told you why, having had this person's evidence since 1993, and why, having admitted that since it was in the OTP's hands since that time, apparently, it wasn't noticed. Mr. Nice explains that he was not known to the OTP, except by a NordBat document, which they didn't recognise the significance of. I don't know more about that. It's a rather amorphous statement by the Prosecution, in response to Your Honours' query. And I suggest that the Prosecution, since 1993, 1994, certainly before Mr. Kordic's original indictment, certainly after his second indictment, and certainly before they prepared this case, had the opportunity to look for these witnesses, their documents and things, and should have done so. We are now faced with a growing number of inches or feet of documents. We are now up to five feet, two metres of documents served on us by the Prosecution. International armed conflict documents, village binders, we are still fighting the village binder issue. They still include statements and an overview by the prosecuting authority. We are still required to look at all of them. So instead of winding this case down, preparing our case, and moving on to other things, we are dealing with these late minute applications. Now, we can read a statement, we can analyse it, and we can get going on it. I'm not saying we can't. But in the throws of where we are in this case, it's wearing to the point of being prejudicial. So, for those two reasons, prejudice, and the fact that this is a six and a half year old statement, we object to this witness being called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How long was he with NordBat?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: According to his statement, Your Honour, he was there six months. That's paragraph 33. "I lived in their camp for the next six months."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You say six and a half year old statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: No, no. I'm sorry, the statement was taken in January, the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You mean it deals with events six and a half years ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's right. And the identity of this individual, his co-operative nature, indeed he was turning over to NordBat documents in 1993, that's set out at paragraph 28 of his statement. That's been extant for a long time. Now, I am tempted to run on and talk about our discussion we had about exculpatory evidence, and searching for it, and affirmative obligations. I understand masses of paper and volumes of boxes and the difficulty, but the Prosecution has acknowledged that they had this witness in their hands, if you will, in the NordBat files. Someone apparently even saw his name, but didn't recognise his significance. There has to be an end. I am reminded, of course, that your order of May 17th required the Prosecution to set out -- yes. That the Prosecution was required by May 17, as per your April 1 order, I believe, to give us all the witnesses that they had. So certainly a thorough search should have and ought to have been done at that time, similar to, if you will, a search for exculpatory evidence, which we have debated. There just has to be a cut-off, there has to be a time, and the Prosecution has to be held accountable. That's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I correct a number of things that have been said there. First of all, we must excise all reference to the documents. They have got nothing to do with this case. The documents that are being provided now, are being provided in the part, of course, of a different exercise. Statements, were it not providing -- I'll just deal with it now, although it's got nothing to deal with the application, I might as well just deal with it. When we are asked not to provide statements to the Defence, that are duplicates of statements, they are now requiring us to serve them. So a large proportion of the material that they now have, and now apparently want, will be duplication. No, we are not serving overviews or summaries of village witness binders. What we've said is that the indices were prepared separately, and they identify that a summary has been prepared. It hasn't been served on the Defence nor on the Court, because we checked what was at one stage thought to be an ambiguous ruling with one of your staff, and they haven't been served thereafter. So that's simply a diversion. It's got nothing to do with this very important application. Further, when Mr. Stein says that this witness was providing statements to NordBat, I am not quite sure I follow what he is referring to, because I don't see that in the statement at all. What happened was that he, according to his own statement, was given a document authorising him to make arrests, and he handed that to NordBat. He didn't make statements. And he was, no doubt, then protected by NordBat, because he was a man under threat of arrest by those who wouldn't be very pleased, perhaps, with what he had done. Mr. Stein then says, "We saw his name." That's not true. I explained to the Chamber that following discovery of his name, in the way I described, we just checked every document that we could, by electronic databases and so on, to see if his name appears at all. It happens to appear somewhere, and I still don't know precisely where, as a listed name. There are loads of names in loads of statements. There is no suggestion that the name shows up as of any significance. And the originating NordBat document, whatever it is, whether it's a statement or a report or something of that sort, itself plainly didn't have relevance for our inquiry. And it's absolutely ridiculous to suggest that that, in any way, makes this an untimely application. This was a man simply not known of by us. And it would be nice to think that people, in the former Yugoslavia, simply volunteered to come and help the Tribunal. They don't. Very occasionally they do, but for the most part they don't. They keep quiet until somebody approaches them. And the means by which they are discovered vary. So this man was unknown to us, there was absolutely no way he could or should have been known to us, unless we stumbled upon him and for some reason picked up a name and gone on and spoken to him. And that simply isn't something we can do, nor something we should be expected to do. The statement is, of course, of enormous importance. I accept that. If accepted, it clears up some of the otherwise uncertainty that might exist about the history of Stupni Do. Stupni Do, the second largest event that you are concerned with in this trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, to which paragraph, particularly, are you referring to? What, in your opinion, are very important or which adds something new, compared to what we had before? Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Almost everything from -- on this particular topic, almost everything, from paragraph 19 onwards, provides first-hand, and with clarity, material that is either new or detailed, and that simply wasn't available before. Can I remind the Chamber, and this is one of the reasons I was slightly reluctant about dealing with this this afternoon, because I hadn't done a comprehensive check, but can I remind the Chamber of some of the things that have been advanced so far on behalf of the Defence about Stupni Do. It's been advanced that the village was defended. It's been raised that the events there were linked to crime, and to the use of the place as a black market centre. It's been suggested that this was a case of excesses in the course of inter-communal fighting, and that it was the result of what has been described as fighting in a built-up area. And there's been some heavy reference made to the fact that the inhabitants were warned and declined to evacuate themselves from their area. Now, that's the way the issue's been joined. There has been somewhere some suggestion, and I haven't yet tracked it down, that the attack on Stupni Do was indeed a form of calculated ethnic cleansing; that is to say, if you attack the Muslims with sufficient ferocity in a place where the Croats are already vulnerable, then you will drive the remaining Croats from the town and thus comply with your overall plan of dividing the ethnic groupings. There's been some evidence of but not a very great deal. And one of the features of Stupni Do is that away from this court, to some degree, and in the ordinary talk about the place, that possibility is one of the competing theories for why it happened. We now see, to return more directly to His Honour Judge Bennouna's question, that paragraph 19, first there is the plan that the local Croats should combine with the local Serbs, but the local Croats were resistant to that, and they sent a letter to Grude saying that they didn't require the assistance of the Serbs, they would seek safe passage via Serbia territory for their injured, and an order coming from Grude was apparently signed by Dario Kordic; new and extremely important, even if it was signed on behalf of someone else. That response, paragraph 20, was not accepted, and thus it was that Ivica Rajic, the indicted person from Kiseljak, arrived. He arrived via Serb territory with units of whom you have heard insofar as the Apostoli and Maturice have been referred to. I'm not sure that the Sioux have been. It sets out what we've already known a little of about Rajic, and Rajic says he'd been sent there by Kordic and Praljak. I pause to observe.
