I haven't had a chance to check against the papers lodged in relation to Rajic, even if they'd be available to me -- I'm not sure they would be -- for the confirmation of his indictment, but this statement is highly likely to be a central statement, if not the central statement, in that case if that man is eventually arrested. 21, Grude wanted to evacuate the Croat population from the town, and in later discussions, Rajic told the witness that there was an agreement between Croatia and Serbia whereby Vares, Zepce, and Kiseljak were to go to the BH Army because they weren't part of the overall plan. 22, he deals with the visits of Kordic to Vares. I think there's been cross-examination to the effect that there was one and only one visit by him there. So that's new, hard, and challenged evidence or will be evidence that is to be challenged. On the 20th of October, the three names were arrested by the HVO, and at a later meeting conducted by Rajic, there were the Commanders of those three special units. 24 is, of course, is a central paragraph. Rajic claimed he had an order by Praljak, Kordic, and Boban, which he held up for people to see. The witness read the order. The order said that the passage had been provided to Croats via the Republika Srpska, in exchange for a territorial concession, and that Croats should move out, it says, of Central Bosnia, but that may need some amplification. The transport was to be provided by Herceg-Bosna and Vares. The Muslim men and the remaining Serbs should be arrested and detained in the high school centre, and we've heard quite a lot about that. We've heard indeed about the named family. Then this: Three Muslim areas named should be taken. At that stage, one of the people present interrupted and said, "These places are too far away. We have an enemy right here in town." Rajic left the meeting, made a phone call, returns and says, "The priority is to arrest Muslims. Stupni Do should be taken." This is all additional material and which simply illuminates, from the position of an insider, what happened. The order stated that the three units were to help the places under threat of attack, and they're named again, and then deals with the replacement of the military leadership. The names that are spoken of there as being replaced are names either for the most part or all of which you've heard. There may be an issue arising in relation to what this witness says or what you've seen already in a document number 1258 about when this replacement occurred, whether it occurred before or at the time of Stupni Do or afterwards. But in any event, there's a little bit of evidence about those last couple of sentences that this witness would appear to be in a position to amplify. 25 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, I didn't ask you to give us the whole testimony in detail, because I think there's something in the procedure that I can't quite grasp without entering into the details of a future testimony, which we don't know whether it will take place or not. So my question was of a general nature, without entering into detail. I think we have had sufficient information. I simply asked for an indication, rather than delivering a whole speech about that testimony. I think we can stop there, as far as I am concerned at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One matter which must be of concern is if we were to grant this, and we haven't discussed it, and of course, we may not, but if we were to grant it, how many more such applications are we to be faced with?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That question needs an answer in two parts, and I'd like to make it, but just to conclude with His Honour Judge Bennouna's point, of course paragraph 26 is critical, because it does unlock the history. And 29 explains something that needs explaining. I think there's a word missing there, but, nevertheless, the sense is clear. The Chamber will recall that there has been evidence of, I think, one HOS insignia found on the ground. You may have thought at the time odd that an insignia should simply be deposited, and that's the explanation for that. It was a deliberate plan. Dealing with Your Honour's question, and I say it comes in two parts, I think the answer is: None. I'll be corrected by Mr. Scott and Ms. Verhaag; I'm not sure of any outstanding inquiries that -- there are other witnesses to be considered, but I'm not sure of any other outstanding inquiries that are likely to lead to applications of this type, but I'm very concerned that there should be no implication or suggestion that the applications are in any way to be associated with error or under-performance by the Prosecution, not at all. On each occasion with these matters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think that suggestion has been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You made it plain that it was a new witness, although the Defence contests that, but your case is this is somebody who wasn't known to you at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case, may I simply conclude in this way, because the importance of this particular -- before I move to my closing remarks, I must just check. Would you give me a minute with my colleagues. I don't want to overlook anything outstanding since you asked the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: May I take this opportunity. We have a 35-paragraph statement. The paragraphs that Mr. Nice is reading apparently are less different than the ones I have numbered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you referred to paragraph 33. I thought you were referring to something else. It's paragraph 30 in our statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Ah, well, ours are differently numbered for some reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's something, which if necessary, will have to be straightened out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Beg your pardon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Being generous to you. You have more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you've now had a chance to consult. Any more witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think there are no other witnesses that fall into this category. There are other witnesses to be dealt with like the tape and the Mr. Hadzihasanovic, but there is nothing that falls into the category --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are witnesses who were on the original list.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Hadzihasanovic wasn't, the tape witnesses weren't because the tape hadn't been discovered, but by and large, I think other witnesses who have been known. I'm not even sure that there are any more outstanding applications, but my very respectful suggestion to the Chamber would be that, of course, each application has to be looked at on its own, and that this one matches precisely the principles that were applied when we looked at the witness who was added last week in relation to the checkpoint, that not to take this evidence, and I've only looked at half of the statement, the other half is also critical to an understanding of what happened, but not to take this evidence will be to oblige yourselves to act on inference from exiguous material where plentiful material now exists, that it makes your task much more difficult not to take the evidence, and indeed it makes for uncertainty where certainty -- or it may make for uncertainty where certainty is available, especially leaving us to argue from inferences without the guidance of evidence that would have been called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, while my own philosophy is that procedure must subserve the wider purposes of substantive law, there is a virtue in procedure, in time limits, that the discipline and the rigor, which is called for, allows the Chamber to organise its work, and I don't think we should overlook that. I mean, I would be very concerned if a week before the estimated closing dates of the Prosecution's case, the Prosecution were to make similar requests. So I think the President's question is very important, to ascertain whether we are really at the end of requests of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be on that particular topic, but were we to debate the matter freely and fully, Your Honour and I would have slightly different views. Because the mission of this institution is to establish the truth. And, indeed, those on this side are only concerned to lay before you the material that will enable you the best to get at the truth. We are not here to win, as I've said before and repeat. Our function is quite specific. And therefore, and I must underline this, a witness like this arising, doesn't arise, so far as I can judge, through any shortfall in the professional performance of all those involved and, indeed, you will know, because I have said it in their praise on many occasions. To get the best evidence to you in this Tribunal involves a huge amount of work, by dedicated people, large chunks of it never paid. And the people are working from 7.30 until 10, seven days a week, to get this material to you. And so that it is very important, that although timeliness and procedure is, of course, a proper concern, and perhaps particularly a concern in a true adversarial setting, where you've got people concerned about the passage of money from pocket to pocket in a civil case, then shortcomings in procedure may more properly be visited on the person whose shortcoming it is. But whereas here the mission is different. I would very respectfully say that the priority has to be getting the best evidence. And it is almost an overriding priority, although, of course, procedure has its part to play. And can I invite you to judge that proposition of mine in this way. First, of course, you could put a parallel for Ahmici, because Ahmici is even more famous. I mean, if a witness were to come who, as it were, had been the right-hand man until shortly before of the person involved in leading the attack, would it not really be your duty to listen to that evidence, rather than to say, for any procedural reason that it should be excised. In our submission, it would, in fact, be the Chamber's duty to listen to it. Viewed another way, and knowing that we do -- Rajic, for example, is not yet arrested. It's hoped that he will be. There's one other thing I must say. If Rajic isn't arrested, the people of Stupni Do are entitled to the best answer, at any trial where this matter is litigated, to the question that is reflected in the memorial they put up for their 38 dead. Of course it's a memorial that speaks of genocide, but they regard this in their village as the seminal event. It's a village which is being rebuilt. The memorial is in stone, and it may be there for years, centuries. How wrong it would be, with great respect, Your Honour, if in 100 or 200 years time people say, "Well, was it what's alleged?" And they will say, "We never knew because, by chance, the witness who could have been heard by the Tribunal, whose findings we know about, wasn't located until a rather late date." The greater interest must be in having this evidence, and the consequences of not having it will be grave for the various missions that we are all engaged in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Nice, we've got the point. We could have heard the witness, I suspect, in this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. There it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, will you now put on your headset. I am sorry to force you to do that, but I do understand what you are saying in English, while speaking French. But what you are saying, and what worries me, is you said that the important thing is to arrive at the truth, and it is the duty of us all that the truth be established. Of course, within the framework of the available means and possibilities of the Tribunal. What I am trying to say, very briefly, is that the possibility that was offered you was offered you within the time frame allotted for the Prosecution's case, which, as you know, has been set, and you accepted it, even though you objected to it, sometimes rather vehemently, but you agreed that these terms should expire on the 10th of March. Now, we should like to let you know that this is not subject to change, and that, therefore, the truth has to be pursued with all the means, but by the deadline which has been set for the 10th of March. And I repeat it once again, that in spite of your work, which we have accepted, and I am saying that it is out of the question to change the deadline by which the Prosecutor has to finish the presentation of his case, and that is the 10th of March. That is what I wanted to say. Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Having considered this case over an extended period of time, and also this witness statement, we are satisfied that the evidence is potentially of importance and of probative value under the Rule. The weight, of course, will be for us to determine. We are also satisfied that this was not a witness who was known to the Prosecution before last month, and therefore it's in the interests of justice to call the witness. There would be no prejudice to the Defence, providing they have the opportunity to prepare for the witness, which they would have. It's part of the duty of this Tribunal to try and establish the truth, and it would not affect the fairness of the trial, to have this witness called. Indeed, it may make the trial fairer, in the sense of enabling the Prosecution to put their full case. On the other hand, we underline what has just been said, that the 10th of March is the date by which the Prosecution must finish their case, in our view. There is great concern about the length of time which these trials are taking, and it's our duty to ensure that they be dealt with as expeditiously as possible. For those reasons, we shall allow this witness to be called. If there are any more applications, of course we will consider them, but we have noted what the Prosecutor has said about the likelihood that there will be none. And, in fact, that is a course which we would support. There is one other aspect of the matter, which I do want to deal with, although it's rather late. And that is the references to five and a half feet of material. Even allowing a little exaggeration, that does seem to be a very large amount to be serving at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As I said, the material is in part duplicative, in that it is re-submitting statements that have already been submitted earlier. We've, I think, revised the procedure, so that now statements are indexed and not actually provided. The quantity of material provided, of course, is the material that is necessary to provide, if we are to attempt resolution in a timely way of the issues about the villages. I've just had a letter from the Defence about the Kiseljak binder. I'll try and deal with it overnight, and raise with the Chamber any issues that arise tomorrow. But I'm afraid that the necessity of making the material available does require there to be quite a lot of material, quite a lot of copying. I wish it were otherwise, but nothing has been admitted and, therefore, everything has to be approved. Can I raise a couple of other matters while we are here? I don't know if there is anything else on that, that the Chamber wants from us. I was going to -- I was going, impertinently, to go back to my exchange with Judge Robinson. I said, right at the beginning of the case, I wouldn't use the words "with great respect," for fear of the fact that it might infer that I meant the reverse. On this occasion, I found I used the phrase twice, and I meant it, because I did understand the genuine concerns for different approaches to procedural matter. But I thought I would make that quite clear. Right. Amongst the other issues that we have, one of them is a witness who I -- can we go into private session, briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He appears -- and then after him appears the Vares witness. Is that the witness we've been dealing with?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure which list Your Honour is now looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm looking at the most recent one, which at the bottom refers to a Vares witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't have the exact copy Your Honour has. I'll just look at it on the screen. Yes. That's correct. That's the witness now identified to the Chamber. Just to bring the Chamber up to date with the rest of the week, I'm going to be informed this afternoon if the tape witness is going to be here. I hope he will be here on Wednesday afternoon. I don't know. I should tell the Chamber and my learned friends that the witness who produces the front-line maps will be available later this week. We'll get a report to them as soon as we can. I think that the outstanding issues that might conveniently be dealt with -- I don't know whether it's possible for them to be dealt with today -- the outstanding issues to be dealt with really relate to the transcript witnesses who we listed on the 10th of November, in the separate annex at the back, and there are some seven witnesses. We've had no response in respect of any of them save for number six, and, of course, he was called, Colonel Stewart. And we've had a response about number seven, which we may be able to deal with which by agreement, but I don't think we've had any responses in relation to the balance. Oh, yes. That's right. Number eight, we are told, is a witness who is required but not with any reasons given. And number eight, incidentally, is a witness who Mr. Scott will be able to deal with, because he is a witness who requires some sensitivity of treatment, like Witness AA did, probably not quite the same regime but not dissimilar, and Mr. Scott's the person on our team able to deal with all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I notice in the document you refer to where you set these witnesses out, that there are references to the accused in these transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein or Mr. Sayers, can you give us an answer on these transcripts? I don't think we want it now, it's late, but could you put it into writing by, say, the end of the week?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We can do that. And let me just correct an error. I said we did not know the identity of these eight witnesses earlier. Apparently, we did; I had just forgotten. But we can certainly present the Court with -- or the Prosecution with a written response to this by the end of the week if that would be possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. While the Defence are dealing with matters, there's one matter that I want to raise with them. Mr. Stein, from time to time you have been submitting that your case would be shorter if you had a longer break after the Prosecution. We are now in the position that we are considering how long that break should be. We shall not, it appears, be taking another case. Therefore, the in the normal course of events, we would want to get on with this case as expeditiously as possible, but so far, I don't think you've explained why you're asking for longer time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Would you like me to now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Why not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Short answer again -- because of my stature I'm answer giving short answers -- whenever I set aside the time or other members of our staff set a time to meet, to confer, to hone down our witness list, to make sure we're not being duplicative and/or set aside the time to meet with co-counsel, it seems like we have another stack of paper to look at, another stack of things to analyse. I won't repeat what Mr. Sayers just said. So instead of focusing now on what should be, we are focusing on wrapping this case up and dealing with the surprises that the Prosecution throws our way at the last minute. So that's the short first version. When this case is behind us or at least towards the end, we will also, of course, be working very hard on, I think, the most important issue now affront, how much of the Prosecution's case will be allowed to go forward. We intend and already have put a substantial effort into that endeavour, and that, I think, will chart our course based on, of course, your ruling and the witnesses that will then be needed if, as I am cautiously optimistic, much if not most of the Prosecution's case is no longer with us. Moreover, there are still witnesses who need to be looked at, spoken with, testimonies made sure, verified, and all the other things we do. It's the old classic, and I'm sure it's not unique to the United States. My brief would have been shorter if I had more time, and that's the identical situation we have here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stein, you come from a pragmatic culture, and I believe you should also endeavour to be pragmatic in this case. When you open your case, you do not have to have everything prepared in advance. You can begin with things which are certain and then to -- then ask the Chamber for a delay so as -- within which you would propose the final list. You know, our problem, because we do not really want to prolong unduly the break, because today the Chamber did not take another case so that we should like indeed to work as expeditiously as possible, in the interests of the Tribunal. If you want to separate things, for instance, to propose a plan so as to begin while still reserving the time to propose the final list of -- the final list while observing a certain number of procedural elements and everything else, that, perhaps, would give you enough time to make a compromise between your concern and our concern, and I believe we should work in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And I appreciate those suggestions, Your Honour. It is my hope, however, that when we present you with your pre-trial statement, it will include all of our witnesses. We won't be asking for applications down the road. It will have everything we need. It is my fondest hope that when we open our case and make our opening address, we will tell you exactly what our case is, with no surprises. Perhaps that's a different approach, different method, but with respect, I'd like to have the book written and then present it to you as opposed to giving you each chapter of manuscript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, I'm not sure whether you have already given an indication, when I wasn't here, but do you have a particular period of time in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I didn't give a specific month or months, as I recall, although I may stand to be corrected. I am corrected, yes. The number of witnesses ran through my head, the months didn't. On the record I had said previously our case would last between five and nine months, and that we had approximately 100 witnesses. I also hedged, as much as I could, because that's a guesstimate, an estimate, and that was the best I could do at that period of time. So the short answer is what you missed is the five to nine months, and the approximately 100 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I meant the time between the close of the Prosecution's case and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. We asked for six weeks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Six weeks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now until tomorrow morning, half past 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
